intro_feedback: The Introduction is clearly present and generally strong for this course level. It opens with societal relevance, defines SAD and the treatment formats, introduces inhibitory learning as the central theoretical framework, and uses the required studies as building blocks toward the research question. The research question and hypothesis are explicit and relevant. A clear strength is that the student tries to compare delivery formats rather than merely summarizing studies one by one. The line of reasoning is mostly coherent and scientifically responsible. At the same time, there are some noticeable weaknesses that keep it below the higher range. The paper starts with adolescence-specific relevance, but the study focuses on adults, so the population focus is not fully aligned. The theoretical argument is sometimes repetitive and somewhat overstated, especially where assumptions about accessibility, privacy, and dose advantages are treated as likely benefits without much empirical support. Some transitions are a bit loose, and the phrasing occasionally obscures the logical chain. There are also a few citation/reference inconsistencies. Overall, this is a good Introduction with a clear storyline and a relevant RQ, but it is not consistently convincing enough for an 8 or higher.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and clearly related to the research question and hypothesis. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present, and the basic design is understandable. Important required elements are included: sample size, age, gender proportion, inclusion/exclusion criteria, recruitment, random allocation, compensation, treatment conditions, number of sessions, and the main outcome measure. The section is largely replicable at a student level. Strong points are the attempt to standardize treatment dose across conditions and the reasonably clear description of the three intervention formats. The LSAS is also described with scoring and an example, which is helpful. The main limitations are in precision and completeness. Some details remain vague, such as how exactly randomization was implemented, whether assessors were blinded, and more concrete procedural timing. The Materials section mixes constructs, design, and procedure in a somewhat confusing way. For the LSAS, the student calls it a self-report questionnaire, which is debatable because the LSAS is commonly clinician-administered; at minimum this should have been handled more carefully. Some references or instrument details are incomplete, and a few sentences are awkwardly phrased. Still, the study design is coherent and mostly complete, so this fits around adequate-to-good.
results_feedback: The Results section is mostly correct, relevant, and easy to follow. It includes a demographics table, descriptive statistics for the main outcome, the appropriate mixed ANOVA for the stated design, assumption checks, main effects, interaction, and post-hoc comparisons. This matches the expected course-level structure reasonably well and is clearly modeled on the sample format. The reporting makes the central finding understandable: all groups improved, but in vivo improved more than both VRET conditions, and the two VRET conditions did not differ significantly. That is a solid basis for an adequate-to-good Results score. The main issues are that the section is somewhat less complete and polished than the sample. The assumption checks are reported only briefly, without exact statistics. There are no effect sizes, and the figure is mentioned but not actually shown in the submitted text. The phrase 'significant main effect of time x condition' should be reported as an interaction, not a main effect. The sentence about averaged anxiety across both time points is not the clearest interpretation and is a bit unnecessary given the interaction. There are also some APA and wording issues, but these should not weigh too heavily here. Overall, this is a competent Results section for this level, though not as complete or polished as the stronger examples.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion is one of the stronger parts of the paper. It starts with a clear answer to the research question, states that the hypothesis was only partly supported, and summarizes the main findings accurately. The student then relates the outcomes to prior studies and attempts to interpret both expected and unexpected findings. A particular strength is that the unexpected absence of a difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET is not ignored; the student actively tries to explain it and link it back to differences with prior studies. The section also includes several relevant limitations, future research directions, and broader implications for theory and practice. This is in line with what the rubric values. The main reasons it does not move into the higher range are that some interpretations are somewhat speculative or stronger than the data warrant. For example, claims about the inhibitory learning model being 'most fully realised' in real-life settings go beyond what was directly tested. Some limitations are generic or less well developed than others, and parts of the future directions section become a bit expansive and repetitive. There is also some tendency to frame the theoretical implications too confidently given the relatively simple design and post-only follow-up. Still, the reasoning remains mostly coherent and grounded, and the critical reflection is relevant. Overall, this is a good Discussion for a second-year first paper.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is readable and generally understandable, and the structure of the major sections is clear. The student uses mostly appropriate scientific language and consistent terminology for the main constructs. However, there are frequent language and style problems that noticeably reduce polish. These include grammar and spelling errors, punctuation problems, awkward phrasing, inconsistent capitalization, and several APA/reference issues. Some examples are sentence fragments, incorrect article use, missing commas, inconsistent hyphenation, and citation formatting problems. There are also mismatches between in-text references and the reference list, and several clearly irrelevant references appear in the reference list, which is a notable APA/content-care issue for this category. Paragraphing is mostly functional, but some sentences are overly long or clumsy, and there is some redundancy. Importantly, the language generally does not obstruct understanding, so this should not be graded as insufficient. At the same time, the number of issues is too high for a 7 or above. This therefore fits best in the developing-to-adequate range.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The paper clearly states a relevant research question and hypothesis, includes all required articles, and builds a recognizable line of reasoning from societal relevance to theory, prior research, and the design choice. The student does more than summarize studies: Anderson, Kampmann, Bouchard, and Zainal are used to motivate why comparing self-guided VRET with therapist-guided VRET and in vivo exposure matters. The inhibitory learning model is also used as a genuine framework rather than only being named. The introduction is especially strong in positioning the proposed study as addressing a gap in the literature. What keeps this from the excellent range is that the societal relevance is not always well aligned with the final population/design focus: the paper opens with adolescence, but the study is on adults, which weakens precision. There are also some awkward transitions, minor imprecision, and paragraph-level structure is not consistently tight. Still, the overall scientific reasoning is above average and convincing, so an 8.0 is justified.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and clearly related to the research question, and it contains the basic required subsections. Participants are described with sample size, age, gender, recruitment, random allocation, and main inclusion/exclusion criteria. The intervention conditions are understandable, and the procedure is chronological and reasonably complete. However, this section misses some elements needed for a higher score. The participant description does not include age SD, and compensation is mentioned but not in a very complete/precise way. More importantly, the materials description is incomplete at the questionnaire level: LSAS is described fairly well, but the SCID-5 is introduced without a real instrument description, and not all measures are described with the full set of details expected in the writing guide. There is also some mixing of procedure-like information into Materials, and some details that would help replication remain somewhat broad. Overall, this is a solid adequate Methods section, but not yet in the good range.
results_feedback: The Results section is solidly around the expected course standard. The correct analysis is used for the design, key test statistics and p-values are reported, descriptive tables are included for demographics and outcome scores, and the results are reported at the operational level. The student also includes an outlier check, normality and variance checks, post-hoc tests with Holm correction, and a figure. These are all strengths. What limits the score is that assumption reporting is not fully complete for this type of analysis: for a mixed ANOVA, the section does not discuss all relevant assumptions in a fully correct and complete way, and reporting remains somewhat thinner than the sample results section. The post-hoc reporting is understandable but not especially precise, and formatting of tables/figure captions is below the cleaner sample standard. Because the calibration notes indicate that following the sample closely would be around a 7.5, this section falls a bit below that but remains clearly adequate.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong Discussion and one of the better parts of the paper. The student clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and explains that the hypothesis is only partly supported. All main findings are interpreted at the construct level, and the discussion engages well with the unexpected result that self-guided and therapist-guided VRET did not differ. The comparison with previous research is substantive rather than superficial, especially in the way the student uses limitations of Anderson and Bouchard to explain why the expected therapist advantage may not have appeared here. The theoretical framework is also revisited meaningfully: the student argues that inhibitory learning may depend partly on the richness of real-life contexts, which is a thoughtful interpretation for this level. Limitations are specific and mostly well linked to their consequences, and future directions follow logically from those limitations. The broader societal implications are also brought back in the conclusion. This does not reach the excellent range because the argument is still somewhat long-winded in places, and some interpretations are speculative or stronger than the data warrant. Still, the reasoning is coherent and clearly above average.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally understandable and has a clear overall structure, so it passes comfortably. Scientific language is used throughout, and most paragraphs have a recognizable focus. However, there are frequent grammar, spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and APA issues. Some examples are inconsistent tense, article use, spacing, typo-level errors, citation formatting problems, and inaccuracies in the reference list. There are also awkward sentences and some redundancy that reduce precision. These issues do not usually obscure meaning, so they should not heavily damage the content grades, but they do keep the Language & Style score in the adequate rather than good range. Overall, this is readable and organized, but not polished.

intro_feedback: De introductie is duidelijk bovengemiddeld voor dit cursusniveau. De maatschappelijke relevantie wordt vroeg en passend voor adolescenten met SAS neergezet, kernbegrippen worden uitgelegd, en er is een herkenbare lijn van probleem naar theorie, eerder onderzoek, onderzoeksgat en hypothesen. Sterk is dat de student niet alleen VRET beschrijft, maar ook uitlegt waarom deze interventie specifiek voor adolescenten relevant zou kunnen zijn. Ook de onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen zijn helder en sluiten goed aan op het voorgestelde design. Wel zijn er enkele punten die een nog hogere beoordeling beperken. De literatuur wordt deels nog vrij sequentieel besproken in plaats van echt sterk gesynthetiseerd, en de koppeling tussen theorie en de voorspelling dat VRET beter zou zijn dan iVET had nog explicieter en kritischer onderbouwd kunnen worden. Daarnaast zit er een kleine inhoudelijke onnauwkeurigheid in de bespreking van de kernstudies, bijvoorbeeld in de weergave van Bouchard en het gebruik van jaartallen. Maar overall is de redenering coherent, relevant en overtuigend genoeg voor een goede 8.0.
methods_feedback: De methode is over het algemeen adequaat en duidelijk gekoppeld aan de onderzoeksvraag. De participanten, inclusie- en exclusiecriteria, condities, meetmomenten en globale procedure zijn aanwezig. De beschrijving van de LSAS-CA bevat veel van de vereiste elementen, en de VRET-conditie is redelijk concreet uitgewerkt. Ook is de random toewijzing genoemd en is de wachtlijstconditie correct verantwoord. Tegelijkertijd ontbreken enkele details die voor dit niveau wel relevant zijn voor volledigheid en repliceerbaarheid. Zo wordt niet uitgelegd hoe de randomisatie precies gebeurde, ontbreekt informatie over eventuele beloning/compensatie, en is de procedure nogal beknopt beschreven. Voor iVET is de beschrijving vrij algemeen; juist omdat VRET uitvoerig wordt uitgewerkt, blijft onduidelijker hoe iVET precies gestandaardiseerd werd en hoe vergelijkbaarheid tussen de actieve condities werd bewaakt. Ook is de beschrijving van de diagnostische screening wat slordig geformuleerd. Daarom komt deze sectie uit op een degelijke maar niet bijzonder sterke 7.0.
results_feedback: De resultaten volgen globaal de structuur van het voorbeeld: er is een korte opening, een demografische tabel, assumptiecontrole, een mixed ANOVA, een tabel met gemiddelden per conditie en meetmoment, en een beschrijving van de post-hocvergelijkingen. Dat is positief en voldoende voor een voldoende. Er zitten echter meerdere inhoudelijke en rapportageproblemen in deze sectie. De ANOVA-vrijheidsgraden lijken niet te passen bij het beschreven design en de steekproefgrootte, wat een belangrijk statistisch probleem is. Daarnaast is de tekst over de post-hocs intern inconsistent: er staat dat er bij prebehandeling geen significante verschillen zijn, maar vervolgens worden p-waarden van .007 gerapporteerd voor twee vergelijkingen, wat juist wel significant zou zijn. Ook de formulering van p-waarden en sommige statistische notaties is onjuist of slordig. Verder ontbreekt een echte inhoudelijke rapportage van de figuur en is de verslaglegging soms minder precies dan in het voorbeeld. Omdat de algemene opzet herkenbaar en relevant is, maar de statistische consistentie duidelijk tekortschiet, is 6.5 passend.
discussion_feedback: De discussie is sterk en vormt samen met de introductie het beste deel van het paper. De student opent met een heldere hoofdconclusie, beantwoordt de onderzoeksvraag expliciet, en maakt goed onderscheid tussen ondersteunde en niet-ondersteunde hypothesen. Vervolgens worden de resultaten verbonden aan eerdere literatuur en aan de theoretische mechanismen uit de introductie. Vooral positief is dat de onverwachte bevinding rond iVET niet wordt genegeerd, maar serieus wordt geïnterpreteerd in relatie tot adolescentie, intensiteit van exposure en mogelijke belemmering van leerprocessen. Ook zijn de beperkingen redelijk studiespecifiek in plaats van volledig generiek, en de implicaties voor toekomstig onderzoek en praktijk sluiten aan bij de bevindingen. Een nog hogere score blijft uit omdat sommige interpretaties speculatief zijn en soms sterker worden gebracht dan de data toelaten, zeker gezien de zwakkere resultatenrapportage en het ontbreken van follow-up. Ook had de student nog explicieter kunnen reflecteren op alternatieve verklaringen zoals uitvoering van iVET, meetproblemen of baselineverschillen. Maar binnen dit cursusniveau is dit een bovengemiddeld sterke discussie.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is over het algemeen goed leesbaar, duidelijk gestructureerd en redelijk wetenschappelijk geformuleerd. De opbouw per sectie is logisch, en de lezer kan de hoofdlijn goed volgen. Dat is een duidelijke sterkte. Er zijn wel meerdere taal- en APA-gerelateerde onnauwkeurigheden, maar die belemmeren het begrip meestal niet. Voorbeelden zijn slordigheden in interpunctie en formulering, wisselende schrijfwijzen, enkele typefouten in namen en titels in de literatuurlijst, foutieve of inconsistente jaartallen, en onzorgvuldige statistische notatie. Ook oogt de titelpagina-informatie duidelijk onrealistisch of niet opgeschoond, en de referentielijst bevat meerdere APA-fouten. Omdat de stijl voldoende tot goed is maar niet near-faultless, is een 7.0 passend.

intro_feedback: A strong introduction for this course level. The research question and hypotheses are clear, societal relevance is established early and specifically for adolescents, and the argument generally follows a coherent hourglass structure. The student defines key concepts such as social anxiety, avoidance/safety behaviour, habituation, and inhibitory learning, and uses these concepts to motivate why VRET may be especially suitable for adolescents. The required studies are included and mostly used as building blocks rather than only being summarized. The final design choice (VRET vs. iVET vs. waitlist, pre-post design) is explicitly justified from the literature gap. This places the section clearly in Tier 3. What keeps it from Tier 4 is that the reasoning is not fully tight throughout: some literature descriptions remain somewhat summary-like, the theoretical framework is functional rather than especially nuanced, and one core-study detail is inaccurate relative to the assignment materials (Bouchard year/content). Still, within second-year expectations, this is above average and well argued.
methods_feedback: The methods section is broadly coherent and clearly aligned with the research question, so it passes comfortably at Tier 1. The participants section includes sample size, age, gender, recruitment, and inclusion/exclusion criteria. The design is understandable, and the intervention conditions are described in enough detail to see what distinguishes VRET, iVET, and waitlist. However, several Tier 2 core requirements are not fully met. Compensation/reward is not reported for all participants, inclusion/exclusion criteria are only lightly substantiated, and the questionnaire description is incomplete at the expected checklist level because it does not clearly give an example item and the scoring description is somewhat incomplete/unclear for the total score interpretation. In addition, some procedural information appears in the Materials section, and the Procedure section is rather brief and does not fully describe the study from start to finish with sufficient timing/detail. Because the section is coherent but misses multiple required Tier 2 core elements, a 6.0 is appropriate.
results_feedback: This is a solid results section at an adequate level. The student reports a suitable mixed ANOVA for the stated design, gives the main effects and interaction with test statistics and p-values, includes demographic and outcome tables, reports an outlier check, mentions assumption checks, and includes post-hoc comparisons with Holm correction. The section is written at the operational level and generally follows the expected sample structure. However, it does not quite reach Tier 3. Some reporting is inconsistent or incorrect: the degrees of freedom for the mixed ANOVA appear implausible for the described sample/design, the normality check is only described briefly and incompletely, and there is a contradiction in the post-hoc section where p = .007 is called non-significant without clear explanation of the corrected threshold. Table/figure formatting is also weaker than the sample standard. So this section is above passing and around average-to-good for this course, but not at the strong 7.5+ level.
discussion_feedback: A strong discussion for this level. The student clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and explains that the hypotheses were only partially supported. The findings are interpreted at the construct level, linked back to prior literature, and the unexpected null result for iVET is not ignored but discussed in a meaningful way. The theoretical framework from the introduction is revisited through habituation and inhibitory learning, and the student gives a plausible account of why VRET may have worked better for adolescents in this design. Limitations are specific rather than generic, and future directions follow logically from them. The broader practical implication for accessibility of treatment is also clearly connected back to the introduction. This satisfies Tier 3 core criteria. It does not quite reach Tier 4 because the discussion is still somewhat segmented and does not systematically weigh alternative interpretations in depth. But it is clearly above average.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and appropriately scientific in tone. Paragraphs usually have a clear focus, section structure is easy to follow, and transitions are mostly smooth. This supports a Tier 2 judgment. The main reasons not to score higher are APA and language accuracy issues: there are multiple reference-list inconsistencies and typos (for example author/year inaccuracies, spelling errors, punctuation inconsistencies, and some formatting issues), and some statistical notation/reporting is not fully correct. There are also occasional awkward or repetitive phrasings. These issues do not seriously obstruct comprehension, so they should not weigh too heavily, but they do keep the style from the near-faultless level required for Tier 3.

intro_feedback: The introduction is clearly above average for this course level. It starts with societal relevance, defines the practical problem, and builds toward a relevant research question about self-led versus therapist-led VRET versus waitlist for social anxiety symptoms. The line of reasoning is generally coherent: prevalence and treatment barriers lead into exposure theory, then into VRET, then into the specific gap on self-led VRET. The required studies are discussed and mostly used as building blocks rather than being listed entirely separately. A strength is that the student tries to connect the hypothesis to a theoretical framework, specifically the inhibitory learning model, and uses this to justify why therapist-led VRET might outperform self-led VRET. The hypothesis is explicit and logically linked to the design. What keeps this from an even higher grade is that the literature synthesis is not always equally strong: some critiques of previous studies are a bit simplistic or not fully convincing, and the theoretical reasoning about 'safety signals' is somewhat stretched and not always sharply distinguished from broader treatment-context differences. There are also a few small inaccuracies/inconsistencies, such as referring to Bouchard as 2018 in the text while the reference list gives 2017, and the population focus shifts between SAD diagnosis and 'existing social anxiety symptoms.' Still, the overall argumentative structure is strong and convincingly motivates the study.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is adequate but clearly less strong than the Introduction and Discussion. The general design is coherent and matches the research question: a randomized three-arm trial with pre- and post-assessment comparing self-led VRET, therapist-led VRET, and waitlist. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present, and the reader can broadly understand what was done. However, several elements that the writing guide expects are missing or underdeveloped. In Participants, recruitment and exclusion criteria are described, allocation is mentioned, and some sample information is eventually reported in Results, but important details are incomplete or somewhat confusing. For example, the screening procedure uses the SCID-5-CV but then refers to a cut-off score of 19/40 'following the guidelines' of that interview, which is conceptually unclear. Compensation/reward is missing. The attrition numbers are also not fully transparent: 86 were eligible, 11 dropped out, leaving 75, but the distribution of dropout across conditions is not reported. In Materials, the LSAS-SR is described reasonably well, but developer/reference use is somewhat unusual, and information such as scoring procedure, administration details, and psychometric support could be stronger. The intervention description is too general for solid replication: there is not enough detail about what exactly happened in sessions, how therapist-led and self-led conditions were standardized, what guidance participants received, or how adherence was ensured. Procedure is understandable chronologically, but timings and practical details remain somewhat vague. There is also no dedicated analyses subsection, even though the Results indicate a mixed ANOVA. Overall, this is a pass and reasonably coherent for second-year level, but it lacks enough precision and completeness to move into clearly good territory.
results_feedback: The Results section is passable and mostly understandable, but it remains somewhat rough compared with the sample structure. Positively, the student reports sample size, notes outliers, presents a demographics table and a means table, states the main analysis, reports main effects and the interaction, and includes post-hoc comparisons. The overall structure is recognizable and broadly appropriate for the stated design. That said, there are several issues that keep the score around average rather than above average. The statistical reporting is not always plausible: the F degrees of freedom are extremely unusual for a mixed ANOVA with 75 participants and two time points, suggesting misunderstanding or incorrect copying/reporting. Assumption testing is said to be shown in Table 1, but Table 1 actually contains descriptive sample statistics rather than assumption checks. Sphericity is mentioned even though with only two time points it is not relevant. The wording about 'mean values on the LSAS-SR scores as a measure for the dependent variable' is imprecise. The student also states that there were no dropouts among the 75 participants, which conflicts with the earlier Methods description of 11 dropouts from the 86 allocated. In the post-hoc section, the finding that all three conditions changed significantly over time is reported, including the waitlist worsening, but this surprising pattern is not described as surprising until the Discussion. Still, the section communicates the main outcome pattern clearly enough, and for this level minor reporting issues alone should not dominate the grade. The bigger concern is the internal inconsistency and questionable statistical detail, which lowers confidence.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion is one of the stronger parts of the paper. It opens with a clear answer to the research question and states whether the hypotheses were supported. The student then connects the findings back to both the theoretical framework and prior literature, and importantly does not ignore the unexpected waitlist worsening. That is a substantial strength: the student recognizes that this pattern is surprising, compares it to the earlier studies, and offers several possible explanations rather than pretending it is unproblematic. The discussion also includes multiple study-specific limitations, such as the unexpectedly changing waitlist group, the use of a single therapist, and the restricted treatment format. These are more meaningful than generic limitations. Future research suggestions generally follow from the limitations discussed, and the paper ends by returning to broader practical relevance, especially accessibility and waiting-list problems. What keeps the grade from being higher is that some interpretations are a bit stronger than the data allow. For instance, the explanation in terms of inhibitory learning, variability, and safety signals is somewhat overstated given that these mechanisms were not directly measured. The final practical implications are somewhat enthusiastic and could have been tempered more explicitly by the methodological weaknesses. Also, the discussion could engage even more critically with the fact that the waitlist result may complicate the strength of the conclusions. Still, the overall reasoning is coherent, relevant, and above average for this course level.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and the structure is clear. Sections are in the expected order, paragraphs mostly have a clear focus, and the scientific tone is mostly appropriate. The reader can usually follow the argument without difficulty. This supports a passing to average score. At the same time, the language and style are not yet polished enough for a higher mark. There are quite a few awkward phrasings, grammatical issues, and word-choice problems, such as 'negative effect on social anxiety symptoms' where 'reduction' would be clearer, 'suffering from it' phrasing, occasional overly long sentences, and some redundancy. APA style is inconsistent in several places: year inconsistencies (Bouchard 2018 in text vs. 2017 in references), citation formatting issues, capitalization inconsistencies, and an incorrect reference entry for Wolitzky-Taylor and LeBeau that includes parenthetical material inside the citation. The title page details are also irregular. None of this seriously impedes understanding, so it should not be judged harshly at this student level, but it does keep the writing from the 'good' range. Overall, the language is adequate and functional, with noticeable but not overwhelming issues.

intro_feedback: This is a strong Introduction for this course level. The paper clearly states the topic, explains societal relevance early, introduces a theoretical framework (the inhibitory learning model), discusses the required studies plus an additional self-found article, and ends with a clear hypothesis. The line of reasoning is generally coherent and the studies are used as building blocks toward the research question rather than being only summarized one by one. A clear strength is that the student explicitly identifies a gap: prior VRET studies used therapist-led formats, whereas self-led VRET may help address waitlist-related access problems. The design choice is therefore well motivated. The main limitation keeping this below the excellent range is that some parts of the argument are a bit too absolute or imprecise. For example, the discussion of prior studies occasionally overstates methodological weaknesses, and the societal relevance is somewhat broad rather than tightly aligned to the exact target population and three-arm design. Also, the introduction still reads somewhat as well-connected sections rather than one seamless, fully polished argument. Overall, however, this is above average and clearly in the good range.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is broadly coherent and passable, but it misses several required details from the writing guide and rubric. Strengths are that the overall design is understandable, the participant recruitment and random allocation are described, inclusion and exclusion criteria are given, and the procedure is presented chronologically. The manipulation is also described sufficiently for a reader to understand the broad difference between self-led and therapist-led VRET. However, the section falls short of Tier 2 on important checklist points. The Participants section reports mean age but not the SD there, and compensation/reward is missing. The Materials section describes only one questionnaire, but not fully enough for the rubric: it gives number of items and score range, but does not clearly provide the meaning of minimum and maximum scores in a fully explicit way beyond 'higher scores indicate more symptoms,' and there is no cut-off information for the LSAS-SR. The sample item description is acceptable but still somewhat rough. More importantly, details that would improve replicability are missing, such as how the VR protocol was standardized across conditions, who exactly delivered the therapist-led sessions, and what participants in the self-led condition received in terms of guidance. There is also some inconsistency between the screening description and the measure used later. So this section is coherent enough to pass, but not complete enough for an adequate score.
results_feedback: The Results section is around adequate. It identifies a suitable analysis for the design, reports the main effects and interaction with test statistics and p-values, includes descriptive statistics, reports an outlier check, mentions assumptions, and includes both tables and a figure. It also reports the results at the operational level using LSAS-SR scores, which is important. These are all solid features for this assignment. The main limitations are in completeness and accuracy of reporting relative to the sample Results section. The assumption checks are said to be shown in Table 1, but Table 1 actually contains demographic data rather than assumption-test results. Sphericity is mentioned even though with only two time points it is not really relevant. The ANOVA degrees of freedom are highly implausible given the sample size, which suggests reporting inaccuracies. Post-hoc tests are reported, but the correction method is not stated, so one of the Tier 2 core criteria is not fully met. The figure is mentioned but not actually shown in the text provided, so formatting/placement cannot be credited strongly. Because the structure is fairly close to the expected format and understandable for this course level, the section is still adequate rather than weak.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong Discussion. The student clearly revisits the research question, states that the hypothesis was supported, interprets the findings at the construct level, and connects the results back to the theoretical framework and the cited literature. A notable strength is that the unexpected waitlist increase is not ignored; instead, it is discussed directly and several possible explanations are considered. The limitations are also study-specific rather than purely generic, especially the discussion of the unusual waitlist pattern and the use of a single therapist. Future research suggestions follow logically from these limitations, and the paper returns to broader practical implications, especially the accessibility value of self-led VRET. What keeps the score below the top of the good range or excellent range is that some interpretation remains somewhat speculative and not always tightly anchored in data or prior literature. For instance, the theoretical interpretation about safety signals is plausible but somewhat stretched from the findings, and alternative interpretations are mentioned less systematically than they could be. The section is nevertheless clearly above average and demonstrates good scientific reasoning for this level.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and structured well enough for scientific writing at this level. Paragraphs mostly have a clear focus, transitions are usually smooth, and the argument is easy to follow. The writing is stronger than average in overall coherence, especially in the Introduction and Discussion. However, there are enough language and APA issues to keep the score in the adequate range rather than the good range. There are multiple sentence-level awkward phrasings, occasional grammar issues, some word-choice problems, and several APA/reference inconsistencies. Examples include citation inconsistencies (e.g., Bouchard is cited as 2018 in the text but 2017 in the reference list), formatting errors, and some inaccurate or clumsy phrasing. There are also a few redundancies and places where the style becomes more conversational than scientific. Still, the text remains understandable throughout, and the writing supports rather than obstructs the argument.

intro_feedback: The introduction is clearly above average for this course level. It opens with societal relevance, explains why SAD matters, and connects that relevance reasonably well to the need for more accessible treatment. The paper also includes a theoretical framework, mainly around exposure principles, self-efficacy, and interaction theory, and these theories are used to motivate the comparison between self-led and therapist-led VRET. The required prior literature is mostly discussed responsibly, and the student does more than summarize: they often explain why each study matters for the present design. The final aim and hypotheses are clearly stated. The main limitation keeping this from a higher score is coherence and precision. The argument is sometimes stretched, some transitions are abrupt, several claims are stronger than the cited evidence seems to justify, and there are inaccuracies in study details (for example confusing years and specific designs/findings). The theoretical reasoning is present, but not always fully tight or well integrated. Overall, this is a good introduction with a visible storyline and clear research question, but not yet consistently convincing enough for an excellent score.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is passable but only slightly above the lower end of adequate/developing. The overall design matches the research question: three conditions, pre-post assessment, and a clear main outcome. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present, and the reader can broadly understand what was done. However, several elements that the writing guide specifically expects are missing or insufficiently detailed. In Participants, there is no mean age with standard deviation in the section itself, no compensation or reward information, and allocation is stated only very briefly. Recruitment and inclusion/exclusion are present, but the phrase 'met the criteria for the social phobia scale' is vague. In Materials, the intervention is described with some useful detail, but the questionnaire description is incomplete by course standards: the developer is cited and scoring is partly explained, yet cutoffs are unclear, reliability/validity are absent, and the section incorrectly states that analysis is done through multiple regression as if that belongs to the instrument. In Procedure, the chronological flow is understandable, but exact timing and several practical details remain vague. There is also no separate analysis subsection, despite the writing guide expecting one. So the section is coherent and mostly related to the hypotheses, but important methodological details are missing for solid replication.
results_feedback: The Results section is just sufficient. It contains the basic expected components: the analysis is named, the design is linked to the analysis, a demographics table is included, assumptions are addressed, and post-hoc comparisons are reported. It also interprets the interaction in the correct general direction and connects findings back to the hypotheses. However, compared with the sample Results section, this section is noticeably incomplete and sometimes statistically inconsistent. The ANOVA degrees of freedom appear incorrect for a three-condition mixed design, Table 2 is announced but not actually reported with the means and standard deviations, and the figure is referenced but not shown in the submitted text. There are also reporting issues such as awkward p-value notation and limited detail on assumption checks. Because the sample results section is the main benchmark here, the absence of the full main descriptive outcome table is a substantial weakness. Still, the general pattern of results is understandable and mostly relevant to the stated design, which is why this remains at the passing threshold rather than below it.
discussion_feedback: This is a good Discussion for this assignment level. The opening paragraph clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and indicates which hypothesis was supported and which was not. The student then relates the findings back to previous literature and attempts to explain both expected and unexpected results. Importantly, the surprising finding that self-led VRET outperformed therapist-led VRET is not ignored; it is interpreted and linked back to theory. The discussion also returns to the theoretical framework by weighing self-efficacy theory against interaction theory, which is a strength. In addition, the section contains multiple study-specific limitations and corresponding future research suggestions, rather than only generic limitations. The broader implications are also brought back to accessibility and waiting lists, which creates a good hourglass structure. What keeps the score from being higher is that some interpretations are still too confident relative to the design, and some theoretical conclusions are stronger than the data warrant because the theorized mechanisms were not actually measured. There is also some redundancy and occasional overstatement in the practical implications. Still, the reasoning is coherent, relevant, and clearly above average.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and the overall structure is clear, so the language does not impede understanding. Sectioning is present and most paragraphs have an identifiable topic. That said, there are frequent grammar and phrasing problems, including article use, punctuation, awkward English formulations ('people their lives', 'when only virtual'), inconsistent citation formatting, and several APA issues in both text and reference list. There are also some vague or imprecise sentences, some redundancy, and some inconsistency in terminology and study details. The title page information is clearly not in proper academic format, and statistical notation/reporting also contains errors, though these are penalized here rather than in content sections. Because the writing remains understandable and mostly structured but shows repeated language and APA problems, this fits best in the developing-to-adequate range.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The paper clearly states the research question and hypotheses, includes societal relevance early on, and discusses all required articles plus additional literature. The student does more than summarize studies: the prior research is generally used to motivate the current comparison between self-led VRET, therapist-led VRET, and waitlist. A theoretical framework is also present, mainly through self-efficacy and interaction theory, and these theories are used to justify the hypothesis. The introduction also explicitly argues why this design adds something beyond prior studies, especially by removing the in vivo component and focusing on SAD rather than only public speaking anxiety. The main reason this does not go higher is that the line of reasoning is not fully tight throughout. Some claims are overstated, some transitions are a bit uneven, and there are factual/sloppy inconsistencies in citing the core studies (e.g., years and descriptions). The societal relevance is present but not always well aligned with the exact target population/design. Still, overall this is above average and fits Tier 3 well.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and clearly linked to the research question, so it passes comfortably. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present. The sample size, age range, gender distribution, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and random allocation are described. The manipulation is also understandable: the reader can follow what happens in the self-led, therapist-led, and waitlist conditions. However, several elements expected by the writing guide are missing or underdeveloped. Mean age and SD are not reported in the Participants section itself, compensation/reward is missing, and the inclusion/exclusion criteria are mostly listed rather than justified. The questionnaire description is incomplete for this level: the LSAS is referenced and described, but the format is not fully precise, there is no clear sample item in standard form, and interpretation/cutoffs are incomplete. There is also confusion in Materials, for example mixing measurement with intervention details and stating that improvement is analyzed through multiple regression, which does not fit the reported ANOVA. Overall, this is a passing but below-average Methods section because the essentials are there, yet several checklist elements for Tier 2 are missing.
results_feedback: The Results section is broadly understandable and uses a suitable analysis for the design: a mixed ANOVA with condition and time. Main effects and the interaction are reported, post-hoc tests are included, an outlier check is mentioned, and a demographics table and figure are provided. That gives the section a solid passing basis. However, compared with the sample results structure, there are some substantial weaknesses that keep it below average. The reporting is incomplete and partly inconsistent. Table 2 is announced but the actual means and SDs are not shown in the submitted text, so key descriptive statistics for the outcome are missing. The ANOVA degrees of freedom appear incorrect for a three-condition, two-time design, which weakens confidence in the reporting. Assumption checks are mentioned only generally and not at the level expected in the guide/sample, and no details are given for Levene’s test or any other assumptions. Tables/figure formatting is also incomplete. So this section meets Tier 1 but not Tier 2 as written.
discussion_feedback: This is the strongest section of the paper. The discussion clearly revisits the research question, states whether the hypothesis was supported, and interprets the findings at the construct level. The student compares the findings to prior research, explains the unexpected superiority of the self-led condition, and returns to the theoretical framework by evaluating self-efficacy theory versus interaction theory. There is also a good amount of critical reflection: the student discusses several specific limitations, including age range, lack of follow-up, and the fact that the proposed mechanisms were not directly measured. Future research recommendations are specific and mostly follow logically from those limitations. The broader practical relevance is also brought back in the conclusion. The discussion is not excellent because some reasoning remains somewhat speculative, and some claims are stronger than the data warrant. There are also occasional imprecisions and overextensions in the interpretation. Still, for a second-year first paper, this is clearly above average and fits Tier 3 well.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally understandable and mostly well structured, with clear sectioning and a recognizable scientific style. Most paragraphs have a discernible focus, and the overall argument can be followed without major difficulty. However, language quality is uneven. There are frequent grammar and phrasing issues, awkward sentence constructions, inconsistent terminology, punctuation problems, and multiple APA/reference errors. Some examples include incorrect years, inconsistent study naming, citation formatting issues, and typographical errors. These problems do not usually obscure meaning, so they should not heavily damage content scores, but they do lower the Language & Style grade. Because the paper remains readable and reasonably organized, I would place this around adequate rather than poor.

intro_feedback: The introduction is clearly above average for this course level. It opens with strong societal relevance focused on adolescents, defines the target disorder, and explains why this population matters. The theoretical framework is not just mentioned but actually used to motivate why exposure-based treatments should work, and why VRET might be especially promising for adolescents. The literature review includes the required core articles and an additional adolescent-focused study, and the student generally uses these studies as building blocks toward the research question rather than only listing them. The transition to the aim, research question, design, and hypotheses is clear. What keeps this from a higher grade is that some parts of the theoretical reasoning are a bit overstated or simplified, especially the mechanism by which exposure would 'ensure' positive outcomes, and the discussion of prior findings could be synthesized even more tightly instead of remaining partly article-by-article. Also, one hypothesis is phrased incorrectly relative to the waitlist condition, since a true waitlist would not normally be expected to improve as an intervention condition would. Still, the overall line of reasoning is coherent, relevant, and convincingly argued for this level.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and clearly linked to the stated research question and hypotheses. Participants, exclusion criteria, recruitment, compensation, random assignment, core treatment conditions, measure, and procedure are all present. The overall design is understandable and mostly replicable at the expected second-year level. The Materials section is relatively detailed for VRET, and the dependent variable is described with the developer, item structure, response scale, scoring range, and cutoff, which is good. The main weaknesses are incompleteness and imbalance across conditions: IVET is described much less precisely than VRET, so comparability between the interventions is not fully transparent. Important sample details such as exact mean age and gender distribution are not reported in the Methods itself but only appear later in Results; that is acceptable in practice but not ideal given the writing guide. The procedure is mostly chronological, but some material/protocol detail is mixed into it, and the waitlist procedure is somewhat underdeveloped. There is also no separate analyses subsection explaining the planned analysis, which would have strengthened completeness. Overall, this is a solid, adequate-to-good Methods section with some missing details that matter for replication.
results_feedback: The Results section is solid and closely follows the sample structure, which is the main benchmark for this assignment. It includes a demographics table, a table with mean scores by condition and time, assumption checks, the mixed ANOVA, and Holm-corrected post-hoc comparisons. The reporting is understandable and mostly consistent with the stated design. The student also reports the interaction and interprets it appropriately before moving to post-hoc tests. This is around the level that the calibration summary describes as a good baseline for Results. What prevents a higher grade is that the assumption reporting is somewhat incomplete compared to the sample: not all relevant assumptions are addressed in equal detail, and the central-limit-theorem justification is somewhat shaky because the relevant unit is not simply total N. In addition, the figure is referenced but not actually included in the text provided, and the section occasionally mixes interpretation into reporting. Still, for this course level, the analyses and reporting are mostly correct, complete, coherent, and relevant.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong Discussion for the course level. The first paragraph clearly answers the research question, states which hypotheses were supported and not supported, and gives a usable summary of the findings. The section then relates the findings back to previous literature and to the theoretical framework, including an attempt to explain the unexpected lack of superiority of VRET. That explanatory reasoning is one of the stronger parts of the paper: the student does not simply restate that the hypothesis was unsupported, but proposes a theoretically grounded account involving cognitive avoidance and the possible added value of CBT. The discussion also contains study-specific limitations rather than only generic ones, and the future research suggestions follow logically from those limitations. Broader implications are addressed by returning to the relevance of treatment accessibility and attractiveness for adolescents. The main issues are that some interpretations are more speculative than the data can directly support, especially the explanation of why VRET may have underperformed relative to expectation, and the paragraph about the waitlist is problematic because it treats improvement in the waitlist as expected and supported by prior work, which is not fully convincing and needed more critical reflection. Even so, the reasoning is coherent, relevant, and above average.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and well structured. Paragraphs usually have a clear focus, the section organization is logical, and the scientific register is appropriate for the assignment. The argument is easy to follow overall, which supports the scientific reasoning. There are, however, noticeable language and APA issues. Some sentences are overly long or slightly awkward, there are occasional wording problems and inconsistencies, and there are a few citation and formatting errors (for example punctuation/capitalization inconsistencies, minor naming issues such as Lisek/Lissek and Maisa-Warner/Masia-Warner, and some non-APA presentation details in headings and front matter). These issues do not seriously impede comprehension, so they should not heavily lower the grade, but they do keep the writing from the near-faultless range. Overall this is a competent, above-average student paper stylistically, but not exceptionally polished.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The paper clearly states the societal relevance of SAD in adolescents, defines the target population, presents a research question and hypotheses, and includes all required articles plus an additional relevant article. The line of reasoning is generally coherent and works as a real argument rather than only a list of studies. A clear strength is that prior studies are used to motivate the design choice of comparing VRET, IVET, and waitlist in adolescents, and the student does attempt to explain why findings from adults may not generalize to adolescents. The theoretical framework is present and tied to the hypothesis, especially through conditioning and the argument about comfort and safety in VR. The introduction also positions the current study relative to limitations in earlier work. Why this is not higher: parts of the theoretical framework are somewhat simplified and not always fully precise, some paragraphs are longer and more summary-heavy than necessary, and the overall argument is good but not fully seamless or exceptionally tight. Still, this is above average and comfortably within the good range.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and clearly related to the research question, and all major subsections are present. Participants, materials, and procedure are described in a way that makes the study broadly understandable, and there are several good elements: random assignment is stated, inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided, the treatment structure is described chronologically, and the main questionnaire is named with a reference and basic scoring information. However, the section misses several elements required for a stronger grade. The participants section does not report mean age and SD or gender distribution there; those details appear only in the Results table. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are listed, but they are not really substantiated or justified. The questionnaire description is decent but incomplete for Tier 2 because it does not clearly interpret min/max scores, and the materials descriptions are uneven across conditions. IVET is described much more briefly than VRET, making the conditions less comparable than they should be. Some content that belongs under materials and standardization is not fully developed. Overall, this is a passing section with decent coherence, but it remains somewhat incomplete for this assignment’s checklist.
results_feedback: This Results section is solid and close to the expected sample structure. The correct overall analysis is used for the stated design, main effects and interaction are reported with test statistics and p-values, descriptive statistics are given, demographic information is presented in a table, and means/SDs per condition and time are also presented in a table. The student also reports an outlier check, an assumption check, post-hoc tests with Holm correction, and interprets the interaction clearly. This is already around average-to-good for this course. The main reason the grade does not move into the good range is that the assumption reporting is not fully complete: only normality and homogeneity are mentioned, while for this kind of reporting the section should be more complete and careful. The figure is announced but not actually visible in the submitted text, so I cannot fully credit formatting and labeling quality. There are also some minor issues in phrasing and precision, such as the CLT justification being somewhat mechanical. Still, the section is understandable, coherent, and broadly aligned with the sample expectations.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong discussion for a second-year first paper. The student clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and distinguishes between supported and unsupported hypotheses. All main findings are interpreted at the construct level, and the discussion meaningfully connects the results back to prior research from the introduction. A notable strength is the treatment of the unexpected finding that VRET was not superior to IVET: the student does not ignore it, but offers a theoretically informed explanation involving cognitive avoidance and differences from Bouchard et al. The section also revisits the theoretical framework, discusses specific limitations rather than only generic ones, and proposes future research directions that follow logically from those limitations. Broader implications for treatment attractiveness and adolescent care are also addressed. Why not higher: some interpretive claims stretch a bit beyond what the data directly show, especially around mechanisms like cognitive avoidance and therapeutic alliance, which are plausible but speculative here. The discussion is very good, but not yet fully unified or exceptionally mature enough for the excellent range.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is clearly understandable throughout and generally uses appropriate scientific language. Paragraphs mostly have a single focus, transitions are usually clear, and the overall structure is easy to follow. The writing supports the argument reasonably well, especially in the introduction and discussion. APA referencing is mostly correct and consistent enough for this level. There are, however, enough language and style issues to keep this from the good range: several sentences are overly long, there is occasional awkward phrasing, some terminology is imprecise or slightly repetitive, and there are a few APA/style inconsistencies and small errors in formatting. These do not seriously obstruct comprehension, so they should not weigh too heavily, but they do prevent the paper from feeling polished. Overall, this is an above-average but not near-faultless style performance.

intro_feedback: The introduction is a clear strength of this paper. It opens with societal relevance, defines SAD clearly, explains why better treatment options matter, and then narrows logically to VRET and finally to the specific comparison between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET. The theoretical reasoning around inhibitory learning, expectancy violation, safety behaviors, and self-focused attention is relevant and generally well connected to the hypothesis. The required core studies are discussed, and the additional studies are used meaningfully to motivate the specific design. Importantly, the paper does more than summarize articles one by one: it builds toward the gap that long-term differences between sVRET and tVRET remain unclear. The research question and hypotheses are explicit and well aligned with the preceding argument. What keeps this from the very highest range is that some parts slightly overstate what prior studies can support, and a few transitions remain somewhat smoother than truly excellent. Still, for this course level, this is a convincingly argued and above-average introduction.
methods_feedback: The methods are coherent and clearly linked to the research question and hypotheses. The basic design is easy to understand, participants are described with sample size, age, gender distribution, diagnosis, recruitment, and exclusion criteria, and the procedure gives a clear chronological overview from screening through follow-up. The materials section also explains the key difference between the two conditions while noting what was standardized across them, which is important for this assignment. The main limitation is completeness: several details expected in the writing guide are missing or too brief. There is no information about compensation/reward, inclusion criteria are implied more than explicitly justified, and the outcome measure description is adequate but not fully complete at the level of item example/scoring detail/cutoff information that would strengthen replicability. Some information that matters for implementation is still somewhat broad, such as therapist training, exact randomization handling, and practical details of adherence or stop criteria. So this is a solid, coherent methods section, but not yet fully complete or replicable enough for a higher score.
results_feedback: The results section follows the sample structure fairly well and is clearly above adequate for this course level. It reports the sample used, provides a demographics table and an outcome table, checks assumptions, reports the mixed ANOVA, and includes post-hoc/simple-effects comparisons that match the stated design. The reporting is understandable and the interpretation of the interaction is clear. This closely matches the calibration note that a results section following the sample format is around a 7.5. The main issues are in precision and completeness rather than core logic: some reporting is not fully polished APA/statistics-wise, effect sizes are reported but not explained, the figure itself is only mentioned rather than actually shown in the text provided, and some phrasing is a bit uneven. Also, the baseline difference between groups is discussed statistically but could have been handled a bit more carefully conceptually given the noticeable mean difference. Still, the analyses are relevant, coherent, and mostly correctly reported, so this is a good results section for this level.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong discussion. The opening paragraph clearly answers the research question, states that the hypothesis was partially supported, and summarizes the main findings in plain language. The section then engages seriously with the unexpected finding that the groups did not differ at post-treatment, which is exactly the kind of critical reasoning emphasized in the rubric and calibration summary. The student offers multiple plausible interpretations, relates them to measurement and design choices, and compares them with prior studies rather than ignoring the discrepancy. The discussion also returns to the theoretical framework, especially inhibitory learning and the role of therapist guidance in strengthening corrective learning and reducing safety behaviors. Limitations are present and fairly study-specific, and future research suggestions follow logically from the findings, especially the idea of a structured transition to in-vivo exposure for sVRET. Broader implications are also connected back to accessibility and clinical usefulness. What keeps this just below the highest range is that some interpretations become somewhat speculative, and the critical evaluation could be broader beyond the measurement issue and transition support. Even so, this is a coherent and convincingly argued discussion, and one of the stronger parts of the paper.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and well organized. Paragraphs mostly have a clear focus, terminology is largely consistent, and the scientific tone is appropriate for the assignment. The argument is easy to follow, especially in the introduction and discussion. There are, however, several noticeable style and APA issues that prevent a higher score. The title page and date contain obvious errors, table formatting is rough, some phrasing is awkward or repetitive, and there are occasional punctuation and wording issues. Reference formatting is mostly acceptable but not consistently polished. These problems do not obstruct understanding, so they should not heavily affect the content grades, but within Language & Style they do matter. Overall, the writing is solidly adequate to good, with clear structure but not near-faultless execution.

intro_feedback: This is a strong Introduction for this course level. The paper clearly states the research question and hypotheses, addresses societal relevance early, defines key concepts such as SAD, VRET, sVRET, and tVRET, and includes all required articles plus additional relevant literature. The line of reasoning is coherent: the student moves from societal burden, to treatment barriers, to VRET, to the specific contrast between self-guided and therapist-guided formats, and then motivates the long-term comparison. The theoretical framework is also genuinely used, especially inhibitory learning, expectancy violation, safety behaviors, and self-focused attention, rather than merely named. Prior studies are not only summarized but linked to the current design and gap. The main reason this does not reach the excellent range is that the argument is not fully seamless throughout: some paragraphs are still a bit literature-review-like, and the theoretical references are helpful but not especially original or unusually nuanced. Still, this is clearly above average and fits well in Tier 3.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and sufficiently detailed to understand the intended study, but it misses several elements needed for a higher score. Strengths are that the design matches the RQ, random assignment is described, the two conditions are differentiated clearly, and the procedure is mostly chronological and understandable. The manipulation description is one of the stronger parts: the student explains what therapist guidance adds and what remains standardized across conditions. However, the section falls short of Tier 2 on some core requirements. The participants section does not report compensation/reward, and the inclusion/exclusion criteria are listed but only minimally substantiated. In Materials, only the LSAS-SR is described in detail; there are not multiple questionnaires here, so that is not a major issue, but the procedure introduces adherence logging and cybersickness checks that are not really described as materials first, which weakens placement and structure. Some references are also embedded in the Materials and Procedure in a way that blurs description and justification. Overall, this is a solid passing-to-adequate Methods section, but not yet in the clearly good range.
results_feedback: The Results section is strong and closely follows the sample structure, which is exactly what the course expects. The correct statistical test is used, descriptive statistics are presented in tables, outlier and assumption checks are reported, and the main effects, interaction, and post-hoc comparisons are described clearly and at the operational level. The reporting is easy to follow, and the follow-up pattern is communicated effectively. This section is above average for this assignment. What keeps it from scoring higher is mostly completeness and formatting. Figure 1 is mentioned but not actually shown in the text provided, so I cannot fully count that as correctly formatted and clearly labelled. In addition, the assumption reporting is adequate but not fully complete in the most rigorous sense, and the effect size notation/reporting is somewhat limited. Still, because the structure matches the expected sample closely and the interpretation of the post-hoc tests is clear, this fits Tier 3 at the lower end.
discussion_feedback: This is a well-developed Discussion and one of the strongest sections of the paper. The student clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and specifies that the hypothesis was only partially supported. Importantly, the paper does not stop at restating findings: it interprets the contrasting trajectories of sVRET and tVRET, discusses the unexpected lack of a post-treatment group difference, revisits prior literature in a substantive way, and connects the findings back to the theoretical framework of inhibitory learning and expectancy violation. The limitations are relatively specific rather than generic, especially the concern about relying on a single self-report measure with overlap between training and assessment context. Future research suggestions also follow logically from the limitations and findings. The discussion also returns to societal and clinical implications in a measured way. The reason this is not in the excellent range is that some explanations remain somewhat speculative, and the discussion, although coherent, still reads partly like a set of well-executed required elements rather than a fully seamless argument. For this course level, however, it is clearly above average.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and appropriately scientific in tone. Paragraphs usually have a clear focus, transitions are mostly smooth, and terminology is used consistently. The writing supports the argument well enough for the reader to follow the logic throughout. APA referencing is mostly correct, and grammar/spelling errors are few. However, there are noticeable issues that prevent a higher score: some awkward phrasing appears, there are formatting problems in the Results tables/figure captions, and the title-page style details are odd or clearly incorrect (for example the impossible due date). There is also some redundancy in the Discussion, and the style is not yet near-faultless. Overall, this is an adequate to good style performance, but more careful polishing would be needed for the good range.

intro_feedback: De introductie is duidelijk bovengemiddeld voor dit cursusniveau. Er is een heldere opbouw van maatschappelijke relevantie naar theoretisch mechanisme, vervolgens naar beperkingen van IVET, de mogelijke meerwaarde van VRET, en uiteindelijk naar de specifieke vraag over adolescenten met SAS. De onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen zijn duidelijk en logisch afgeleid uit de besproken literatuur. Ook is er zichtbaar geprobeerd om studies niet alleen los samen te vatten, maar te gebruiken als bouwstenen voor het argument. Sterke punten zijn de duidelijke focus op de doelgroep adolescenten, de koppeling aan een theoretisch mechanisme van vermijding en zelfgerichte aandacht, en de expliciete motivatie voor de drie condities. Wel zijn er enkele inhoudelijke onnauwkeurigheden die de score net onder excellent houden. De student gebruikt niet alle kernartikelen precies zoals in de opdracht bedoeld: Anderson et al. (2013) ontbreekt in de inleiding, Kampmann et al. wordt inhoudelijk deels verward met een ander artikel/jaartal, en Bouchard wordt in de tekst als 2017 genoemd terwijl in de literatuurlijst 2016 staat. Daarnaast is de theoretische redenering soms wat speculatief en niet altijd scherp gescheiden van empirische bevindingen. Toch blijft de lijn van redenering coherent, relevant en overtuigend, waardoor een 8.0 passend is.
methods_feedback: De methode is voldoende en coherent, maar duidelijk minder sterk uitgewerkt dan de introductie en discussie. Positief is dat het design goed aansluit bij de onderzoeksvraag: drie condities, pre-postmeting, random toewijzing, duidelijke inclusie- en exclusiecriteria en basisdemografie zijn aanwezig. Ook is de procedure per conditie redelijk goed chronologisch beschreven. Dat maakt het geheel begrijpelijk. Tegelijk ontbreken meerdere elementen die volgens de schrijfwijzer eigenlijk wel verwacht worden. De materialen zijn te summier beschreven: de VRET- en IVET-interventies worden inhoudelijk nauwelijks uitgewerkt, er wordt vooral apparatuur genoemd in plaats van de manipulatie zelf. Er is weinig informatie over welke virtuele of echte sociale situaties precies gebruikt werden, hoe standaardisatie tussen condities werd gewaarborgd, en hoe therapeuten volgens protocol werkten. Voor de LSAS-CA worden ontwikkelaars, itemaantal, voorbeelditems en scoring goed beschreven, maar informatie over betrouwbaarheid/validiteit ontbreekt. Belangrijker is dat allocatie, beloning/compensatie en analyseplan ontbreken of nauwelijks beschreven zijn. Ook is de procedure van de wachtlijstconditie minder precies qua timing. Voor dit studentniveau is de methode nog voldoende compleet om het onderzoek in grote lijnen te begrijpen, maar niet sterk genoeg voor een hogere score.
results_feedback: De resultaten zijn over het algemeen begrijpelijk en sluiten aan bij het design, maar blijven qua uitwerking en rapportage onder het niveau van het meegegeven voorbeeld. Positief is dat de student een passende mixed ANOVA gebruikt, de hoofdeffecten en interactie rapporteert, een tabel met gemiddelden en standaarddeviaties geeft, en Holm-gecorrigeerde post-hocvergelijkingen beschrijft. Ook wordt de hoofdconclusie uit de cijfers correct benoemd: beide actieve behandelingen verbeteren, VRET sterker dan IVET, wachtlijst niet. Dat maakt de sectie functioneel en relevant. Tegelijk zijn er duidelijke tekortkomingen. Er ontbreekt een aparte demografietabel zoals in het voorbeeld verwacht wordt. Assumptierapportage is summier en deels onjuist geformuleerd ('Shaprio-Wilk-assumptie', 'homogeniteit van variaties'). Bij een design met drie groepen en twee meetmomenten is de rapportage van de post-hoc t-toetsen niet altijd transparant of volledig te volgen, en sommige vrijheidsgraden lijken ongebruikelijk zonder toelichting. Daarnaast sluipt interpretatie in de resultaatsectie binnen ('wat in lijn was met de opgestelde hypothese', 'wat afwijkt van de oorspronkelijke hypothese'), terwijl dit meer bij de discussie hoort. De figuur wordt genoemd maar niet echt uitgewerkt, en de rapportage volgt de stijl van het voorbeeld maar slechts gedeeltelijk. Daarom is dit een voldoende, gemiddeld resultaat, maar niet bovengemiddeld.
discussion_feedback: De discussie is sterk en duidelijk één van de beste onderdelen van het paper. De eerste alinea doet precies wat verwacht wordt: het doel en de hypothesen worden herhaald, de onderzoeksvraag wordt beantwoord en er wordt expliciet aangegeven welke hypothese wel en niet ondersteund is. Daarna interpreteert de student de bevindingen in relatie tot eerdere literatuur en theorie. Vooral sterk is dat het onverwachte resultaat — VRET effectiever dan IVET — niet wordt genegeerd, maar uitgebreid wordt besproken met meerdere mogelijke verklaringen. De student koppelt deze verklaringen terug aan adolescent-specifieke kenmerken, het theoretische mechanisme van zelfgerichte aandacht en vermijding, en aan verschillen in therapeutische begeleiding. Ook de kritische reflectie is goed: de mogelijke confound van begeleidingsverschillen wordt expliciet benoemd, er wordt gereflecteerd op wat wel en niet uit de data geconcludeerd kan worden, en toekomstig onderzoek wordt concreet en logisch voorgesteld met een vierconditiesdesign. Daarnaast wordt teruggekeerd naar klinische relevantie en maatschappelijke implicaties. Wat de score net onder excellent houdt, is dat sommige redeneringen speculatief blijven en soms wat langdradig of repetitief worden. Ook is de omgang met de confound niet helemaal scherp: eerst wordt het terecht als alternatieve verklaring besproken, maar later deels geneutraliseerd door te zeggen dat het niet als confound geldt omdat het praktijkconform is. Dat is inhoudelijk niet helemaal overtuigend. Desondanks is de discussie voor dit niveau duidelijk bovengemiddeld.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is over het geheel genomen helder, goed leesbaar en logisch gestructureerd. De paragrafen hebben meestal een duidelijke focus en de opbouw van het paper is gemakkelijk te volgen. Het taalgebruik is passend wetenschappelijk voor een tweedejaarsstudent en de argumentatieve lijn blijft meestal goed zichtbaar. Dat ondersteunt de inhoudelijke kwaliteit van vooral introductie en discussie. Er zijn wel diverse taal- en stijlproblemen die een hogere score verhinderen. Er komen meerdere spel- en typfouten voor, zoals 'Axiety', 'verassend' in plaats van 'verrassend', 'bloostelling', en enkele onhandige of grammaticaal gebrekkige zinnen. Ook is de APA-stijl wisselend: jaartallen zijn niet altijd consistent, er zijn referentie-onnauwkeurigheden en enkele inhoudelijke mismatches tussen tekst en literatuurlijst. De opmaak van de resultatensectie en tabellen/figuurverwijzingen is rommelig, bijvoorbeeld 'Tabel 1Gemiddelde...' zonder nette scheiding. Verder zijn sommige zinnen wat omslachtig of redundant. Omdat deze problemen de begrijpelijkheid niet ernstig ondermijnen, maar wel regelmatig zichtbaar zijn, past een 7.0 goed.

intro_feedback: Een sterke introductie voor dit niveau. De maatschappelijke relevantie staat duidelijk aan het begin en is goed toegespitst op adolescenten met sociale angststoornis. De onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen zijn aanwezig en volgen logisch uit de opbouw. Er is ook een duidelijke theoretische lijn rond vermijding, zelfgerichte aandacht en exposure, en de student probeert theorie echt te gebruiken om verwachtingen over adolescenten te onderbouwen. Verder worden de studies niet alleen los samengevat, maar meestal aan elkaar gekoppeld en gebruikt als bouwstenen richting het eigen onderzoek. Ook wordt de keuze voor vergelijking met IVET en wachtlijst expliciet verantwoord. Wel zijn er enkele beperkingen die maken dat dit nog niet excellent is: niet alle verplichte kernartikelen zijn correct verwerkt op inhoudsniveau. Anderson et al. (2013) ontbreekt feitelijk in de lopende tekst, en Kampmann et al. (2016) wordt in de tekst inhoudelijk verward met Kampmann et al. (2015), terwijl het schrijfdocument juist die specifieke studies voorschrijft. Daarnaast is de argumentatielijn soms wat langdradig en niet overal even strak, met enkele formuleringen die logisch net niet helemaal scherp zijn. Toch is dit duidelijk boven gemiddeld en voldoet het aan Tier 3-niveau.
methods_feedback: De methodesectie is voldoende en coherent, maar duidelijk minder sterk uitgewerkt dan de introductie en discussie.
