Positief is dat de deelnemersgroep, leeftijd, genderverdeling, inclusie- en exclusiecriteria en random toewijzing zijn beschreven. Ook is de globale opzet passend bij de onderzoeksvraag. De procedure is chronologisch en voor een eerste paper redelijk goed te volgen. Toch ontbreken meerdere onderdelen die volgens de rubric en writing guide nodig zijn voor een hoger niveau. Er wordt geen compensatie of beloning genoemd. De beschrijving van materialen is beperkt: alleen de LSAS-CA wordt echt uitgewerkt, en zelfs daar ontbreken enkele gewenste elementen zoals een duidelijke interpretatie van minimum- en maximumscores in relatie tot de schaal als geheel op een volledig uitgewerkte manier. Betrouwbaarheid/validiteit ontbreekt. De onafhankelijke variabelen zijn ook onvoldoende precies beschreven: van VRET wordt vooral de headset genoemd, maar niet concreet welke virtuele sociale scenario’s werden gebruikt, hoe die verschilden of gestandaardiseerd werden. Voor IVET is de beschrijving functioneel, maar ook niet heel gedetailleerd. Bovendien staat procedurele informatie deels onder Materiaal. Daardoor haalt deze sectie vooral Tier 1, met enkele Tier 2-elementen maar niet genoeg voor een degelijke 6.5 of hoger.
results_feedback: De resultatensectie is over het algemeen adequaat en sluit in grote lijnen aan op het verwachte type analyse. De juiste analyse is gekozen voor het design, de hoofd- en interactie-effecten worden gerapporteerd met F-waarden en p-waarden, en er zijn descriptieve statistieken opgenomen. Ook post-hocvergelijkingen en effectgroottes worden vermeld, wat positief is. Daarnaast wordt een figuur genoemd en is een tabel met pre- en postgemiddelden aanwezig. Er zijn echter meerdere tekortkomingen ten opzichte van de voorbeeldresultaten en rubric. De verplichte demografische tabel per conditie ontbreekt. De assumptierapportage is te summier en deels onjuist geformuleerd: er wordt verwezen naar 'de Shaprio-Wilk-assumptie voor normaliteit en homogeniteit van variaties', terwijl homogeniteit niet met Shapiro-Wilk wordt getest, en bij twee meetmomenten is sfericiteit niet relevant maar dat wordt niet helder gemaakt. De rapportage van de uitbijters is ook erg globaal. Verder zijn enkele formuleringen slordig, bijvoorbeeld bij de interpretatie van posttests en in de zinsbouw rond de significante verschillen. Door deze tekortkomingen komt de sectie uit op de onderkant van Tier 2: voldoende tot adequaat, maar niet zo volledig en verzorgd als het voorbeeld.
discussion_feedback: De discussie is sterk en is, samen met de introductie, het beste onderdeel van het paper. De student herneemt duidelijk het doel en de hypothesen, geeft een helder hoofdconclusie, en maakt goed onderscheid tussen bevestigde en niet-bevestigde verwachtingen. Belangrijk is dat de onverwachte bevinding — dat VRET effectiever was dan IVET — niet genegeerd wordt, maar juist uitgebreid en inhoudelijk besproken. De student vergelijkt de resultaten met eerder onderzoek, koppelt ze terug aan de theorie uit de introductie en werkt meerdere mogelijke verklaringen uit, waaronder ervaren controle, adolescent-specifieke kenmerken en verschillen in begeleiding. Dat laatste is vooral sterk: de student identificeert zelf een mogelijk confound en denkt kritisch na over wat het design eigenlijk wel en niet toelaat qua conclusie. Ook de suggesties voor vervolgonderzoek zijn specifiek en logisch afgeleid uit de beperkingen, bijvoorbeeld het voorstel voor een 2x2 design met virtualiteit en mate van begeleiding. Daarnaast wordt de maatschappelijke relevantie weer verbonden aan de klinische praktijk. Het is nog niet helemaal excellent omdat de discussie soms wat herhalend is, enkele claims wat stellig geformuleerd zijn, en de redenering niet overal even compact of volledig systematisch is. Maar voor tweedejaarsniveau is dit duidelijk bovengemiddeld en overtuigend.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is goed leesbaar en over het algemeen wetenschappelijk van toon. De structuur van de secties is duidelijk en de meeste alinea’s hebben een herkenbare focus. De argumentatie is meestal goed te volgen, vooral in de introductie en discussie. Referenties zijn ruim aanwezig en overwegend correct gebruikt. Wel zijn er meerdere taal- en stijlfouten die maken dat dit niet boven gemiddeld goed wordt. Er zijn geregeld spelfouten en slordigheden, zoals 'verassend' in plaats van 'verrassend', 'Axiety', 'bloostelling', onregelmatige interpunctie en enkele onhandige of te lange zinnen. Ook zijn APA-details niet consequent netjes: er zijn kleine inconsistenties in referenties, opmaak van tabellen/figuren is niet verzorgd, en in de tekst staan soms stilistische of grammaticale haperingen. De tekst blijft echter duidelijk begrijpelijk en voldoende wetenschappelijk, dus dit komt uit op een nette 7.0.

intro_feedback:
The introduction is clearly above average for this course level. It opens with societal relevance, defines SAD, explains why treatment matters, and works toward a relevant research question. The paper also includes the required core literature and an additional article, and these studies are used in a reasonably logical sequence to motivate the comparison between therapist-guided and self-guided VRET. The final hypothesis is clear and the design is briefly stated.

The main reason this is not higher is that the theoretical framework is only partly developed. The Pavlovian extinction model is mentioned, but the theory is not really built into a fuller argument about why therapist guidance should matter specifically, or why any difference should or should not persist over time. Some transitions are a bit summary-like rather than genuinely synthetic, and several claims are somewhat overstated or simplified. There are also some inaccuracies relative to the assignment materials, such as citing Kampmann (2015) and Bouchard (2016) instead of the course versions, and the distinction between CBT and exposure therapy is described somewhat loosely. Still, the overall line of reasoning is coherent, responsible, and leads clearly to the RQ and hypothesis, which fits the 'good' range.
methods_feedback:
The Methods section is coherent and generally aligned with the stated research question and hypothesis. Participants, inclusion and exclusion criteria, random assignment, compensation, intervention structure, and the main outcome measure are all described. The reader can broadly understand what was done, and at this student level the study is mostly replicable in outline.

At the same time, there are important missing details that keep the section closer to adequate/good rather than solidly good. The participant subsection is reasonably complete, but some choices are not justified. In Materials, the intervention descriptions are understandable, yet still somewhat underspecified: it remains unclear exactly what scenarios were used, how the virtual therapist operated, how standardized the sessions were across conditions, and what protocol ensured comparability between groups. For the LSAS-SR, the scale, item count, example items, score range, and a psychometric citation are given, which is good, but the developer citation is not provided in the expected way and no cut-off or clinical interpretation is included. In Procedure, the chronological order is mostly clear, but some procedural details are mixed with intervention description, and key timing information is still somewhat rough. There is also a potential confound built into the design: the self-guided group completes treatment at home while the therapist-guided group is treated in-office. The student later recognizes this in the Discussion, but methodologically it weakens the design itself. Overall, the section is complete enough and mostly correct, but not fully precise or controlled.
results_feedback:
The Results section is mostly correct, coherent, and relevant to the stated design. The student reports descriptive statistics per condition and timepoint, uses a mixed ANOVA that matches the repeated-measures two-condition design, reports the main effects and interaction, and follows up the interaction with post-hoc comparisons. The interpretation of the pattern is understandable and consistent with the reported means. This is a solid performance for this level.

The grade is held back because the section does not follow the sample structure as closely as it could. A demographics table is missing, even though the sample results template expects one. The descriptive table is serviceable, but the formatting is rough and includes unnecessary SE values while omitting cleaner presentation. Assumption checks are described only in a general way; no concrete statistics are reported for normality, homogeneity, or sphericity. Outliers are mentioned, but without enough detail about how they were identified. There is also no figure, which is not always essential but would have strengthened the presentation. Minor reporting and APA/statistical style issues are present, but these alone do not drive the grade down. Overall this is around average to slightly above average: analytically appropriate and understandable, but not as complete or polished as the stronger results sections in this course.
discussion_feedback:
The Discussion is one of the stronger parts of the paper. It starts with a clear answer to the research question, states that the hypothesis was supported for post-treatment, and summarizes the main pattern of findings accurately. The student then relates the findings back to prior literature and makes a genuine effort to interpret the unexpected follow-up pattern in the self-guided condition. The section also includes several study-specific limitations rather than relying only on generic criticisms, which is a clear strength.

What keeps the Discussion from an 8 or higher is that some parts remain somewhat surface-level or speculative. The explanation involving self-efficacy is plausible, but it is not strongly tied back to the introduction's theoretical framework because that framework was not fully developed there. The discussion of theory therefore remains limited. Some implications are a bit stronger than the design warrants, especially the conclusion that self-guided VRET may be suitable for people who avoid therapist contact, since the study did not actually measure whether that barrier was present in this sample. Still, the student does acknowledge this later, which helps. The critical reflection is relevant and reasonably convincing, especially the discussion of measurement context and treatment context as possible confounds. Overall, this is a coherent and above-average discussion for a second-year first paper.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and the overall structure is clear. Sections are easy to follow, paragraphing is mostly functional, and the scientific tone is appropriate for this level. The argument is usually understandable without major effort, which supports a passing grade in this category.

However, the writing is not polished. There are repeated grammar and phrasing issues, awkward sentences, spacing inconsistencies, and several APA/reference problems. Examples include inconsistent hyphenation and terminology (for example selfguided, therapistguided, therapist-guided), citation inconsistencies, punctuation errors, and some imprecise wording. There are also a few inaccuracies in references and formatting problems in the Results table and reference list. These issues do not usually obscure the meaning, so they should not be penalized in content sections, but they do lower the Language & Style score. This therefore fits the adequate range rather than good.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The paper clearly establishes societal relevance, defines SAD and treatment approaches, includes the required articles plus a self-found article, and ends with a clear research question, design, and hypothesis. The strongest aspect is the overall line of reasoning: the argument moves from SAD as an important problem, to limits of existing treatments, to therapist-guided VRET, to the potential value of self-guided VRET, and then to the gap of no direct comparison. That gives the study a clear rationale. Prior research is generally used as building blocks rather than only summarized separately. The hypothesis also follows logically from the discussion of therapist support and the possible lack of individualized feedback in self-guided treatment. What keeps this section from the excellent range is that the theoretical framework is somewhat thin and not fully developed as a coherent model linking the variables. The extinction model is introduced, but the mechanism for why therapist guidance should outperform self-guidance is only briefly argued. There are also a few inaccuracies/inconsistencies in study years and some slightly loose wording. Still, by rubric standards this is above average and solidly in Tier 3.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is clearly passing and overall adequate. Participants are described with sample size, mean age, SD, gender distribution, allocation, exclusion criteria, and compensation. The design matches the research question well, and the procedure is mostly chronological and understandable. The manipulation is also described clearly enough to understand the difference between therapist-guided and self-guided VRET, and the randomization method is specified. The main limitation is the Materials section: only one questionnaire is described, which is acceptable here because it appears to be the only dependent measure, but the description is not fully complete at Tier 2/Tier 3 level because the scale description is a bit imprecise and the developer/reference of the LSAS-SR is not introduced as clearly as recommended in the guide. In addition, some procedural details are mixed into Materials and some materials-level detail still appears in Procedure, so the section structure is not fully clean. There are also some choices that are described but not fully justified, such as why the self-guided group took the headset home while the therapist-guided group attended the office. Overall, this is a coherent and reasonably replicable section for a second-year student, but not detailed and polished enough for a higher Tier 3 score.
results_feedback: The Results section is adequate and understandable, with the correct general analysis for the design: a mixed ANOVA with time and condition. Main effects and the interaction are reported with test statistics, p-values, and effect sizes, and the post-hoc comparisons are also described clearly. The section is reported at the operational level using LSAS-SR scores, which is good. The student also reports outliers and assumption checks. However, compared with the sample Results section, some important expected elements are missing or weaker. There is no separate demographics table per condition, and there is no figure showing score changes over time. The outlier reporting is somewhat vague because no rationale is given beyond simply deciding to keep them, and the assumption checks are reported only in a general way without actual statistics. Table formatting is also not very strong and does not fully match the sample style. So this section meets Tier 2 reasonably well, but not Tier 3, where more complete and more polished reporting would be expected. A 7.0 fits well here.
discussion_feedback: This is a good discussion overall. The paper clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and addresses the hypothesis. All main findings are interpreted at the construct level, including the key pattern that therapist-guided VRET was stronger immediately post-treatment while self-guided VRET caught up by follow-up. The discussion also compares the findings to prior studies from the introduction and explains how this study adds something new by directly comparing guided and self-guided VRET. A clear strength is that the unexpected follow-up improvement in the self-guided condition is not ignored; the student proposes a possible explanation involving self-efficacy. The limitations section is also stronger than average for this level: it is specific, relevant to the actual design, and linked to interpretation of the findings. Future research suggestions logically follow from these limitations. What prevents a higher score is that the theoretical framework from the introduction is not really revisited in a fully explicit way. The discussion mentions self-efficacy, but this was not a central part of the introduction’s framework, so the paper partly shifts theory rather than clearly evaluating the original framework. Some explanations are also somewhat speculative and not strongly grounded in cited prior research. Even so, this is a thoughtful and coherent discussion that reaches Tier 3 overall.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and structured well enough to follow. Paragraphs usually have a single focus, and the writing uses scientific language appropriately for this level. The paper has a coherent overall organization from introduction through conclusion. That said, there are quite a few language and APA-level issues that keep the style from the good range. These include punctuation and spacing problems, inconsistent hyphenation and terminology (for example therapist-guided, therapistguided, selfguided), some awkward phrasing, occasional grammatical errors, and several APA/reference inaccuracies or inconsistencies in publication years and formatting. These issues do not seriously obstruct understanding, so the section remains adequate rather than weak. A 7.0 is appropriate: clearly passable and readable, but not polished.

intro_feedback: De introductie is duidelijk boven gemiddeld. De maatschappelijke relevantie wordt vroeg en concreet uitgewerkt, de kernbegrippen zijn goed gedefinieerd, en er is een zichtbare lijn van probleemstelling via theorie en eerdere literatuur naar de onderzoeksvraag. Positief is ook dat de student niet alleen studies opsomt, maar de besproken literatuur gebruikt om de lacune te formuleren: vooral het ontbreken van directe vergelijking tussen zelfgeleide en therapeut-geleide VRET. De drie verplichte studies zijn opgenomen en functioneel gebruikt. Het theoretisch kader met vermijding, inhibitory learning, expectancy violation en presence is inhoudelijk passend en goed gekoppeld aan de hypothesen. Wel blijft de theoretische integratie soms iets beschrijvend en worden sommige claims vrij stellig geformuleerd zonder volledig uit te werken waarom dit specifiek tot verschillen tussen de drie condities zou moeten leiden. Ook had de overgang van algemene theorie naar de precieze designkeuze nog iets scherper gekund. Toch is de redenering coherent en overtuigend voor dit cursusniveau.
methods_feedback: De methode is voldoende en coherent, maar duidelijk minder sterk dan de introductie. De globale opzet sluit aan bij de onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen: de drie condities, pre-post ontwerp en afhankelijke variabele zijn helder. Inclusie- en exclusiecriteria worden genoemd en deels beargumenteerd, en de randomisatie wordt benoemd. Ook is de LSAS-SR redelijk beschreven. Tegelijk ontbreken verschillende elementen die volgens de schrijfwijzer echt verwacht worden. Bij participanten ontbreken gemiddelde leeftijd, standaarddeviatie, genderverdeling, beloning/compensatie en verdere steekproefkenmerken. De Materials-sectie noemt voor de LSAS-SR geen ontwikkelaars van de self-reportversie en geeft geen voorbeelditem of psychometrische informatie. De beschrijving van de interventies is functioneel, maar nog niet precies genoeg om het onderzoek goed te kunnen repliceren: de concrete inhoud van sessies, verschillen tussen condities en de mate van standaardisatie blijven te globaal. In de procedure staat bovendien geen echte chronologische uitwerking van wat deelnemers precies doen vanaf intake tot posttest en de informatie over analyse staat feitelijk in de procedure verwerkt in plaats van apart of duidelijk methodisch verantwoord. Voor dit niveau is het nog steeds een samenhangende en grotendeels correcte methode, maar de sectie mist meerdere vereiste details.
results_feedback: De resultaten zijn over het algemeen begrijpelijk en passend bij het beschreven design. De student rapporteert een mixed ANOVA die aansluit op de onderzoeksvraag, beschrijft de assumptiechecks, geeft de hoofd- en interactie-effecten en rapporteert post-hocvergelijkingen. Ook is er een tabel met gemiddelden en standaarddeviaties per conditie en meetmoment. Daarmee is de basis op orde. Tegelijk wijkt de sectie merkbaar af van het voorbeeld en mist zij enkele verwachte onderdelen. Er is geen demografische tabel, terwijl die in deze opdracht wel als belangrijk referentiepunt geldt. De rapportage blijft vrij summier: er wordt geen aantalsinformatie per conditie in de resultaten herhaald, geen expliciete verwijzing naar mogelijke uitbijters of datacompleetheid gegeven, en de post-hocrapportage blijft globaal. De figuur wordt aangekondigd maar niet echt uitgewerkt in de ingeleverde tekst. Ook is de statistische rapportage niet overal even precies of APA-netjes, maar dat telt hier beperkt mee. Inhoudelijk is de sectie mostly correct en coherent, maar qua volledigheid en aansluiting op het sample results-document gemiddeld in plaats van sterk.
discussion_feedback: De discussie is sterk en duidelijk boven gemiddeld. De eerste alinea geeft een helder antwoord op de onderzoeksvraag en maakt expliciet welke hypothese wel en niet is bevestigd. Daarna worden de bevindingen goed gekoppeld aan eerdere literatuur en aan het theoretisch kader, vooral inhibitory learning en expectancy violation. Sterk is dat de student niet alleen herhaalt dat er geen verschillen zijn gevonden, maar ook alternatieve verklaringen bespreekt, zoals de hoge standaardisatie van de zelfgeleide interventie en de mogelijkheid dat de globale uitkomstmaat subtiele verschillen niet oppikte. Ook de beperkingen zijn relevant en studiespecifiek: geen follow-up, beperkte generaliseerbaarheid en geen meting van procesmaten. De suggesties voor toekomstig onderzoek volgen logisch uit die beperkingen. Wat nog beter kon, is de theoretische reflectie iets scherper maken: de student suggereert implicaties voor het model, maar werkt minder precies uit welke onderdelen van het theoretisch kader nu wel of niet direct getoetst zijn. Daarnaast had de discussie iets kritischer kunnen zijn over de sterkte van de conclusie dat zelfgeleide VRET een gelijkwaardig alternatief is, gezien alleen een pre-postmeting zonder follow-up. Toch is de redenering coherent, relevant en overtuigend voor dit niveau.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is over het algemeen helder, leesbaar en goed gestructureerd. De opbouw per sectie is logisch en het wetenschappelijke register is passend voor een tweedejaars paper. De student gebruikt doorgaans consistente terminologie en de argumentatieve lijn is goed te volgen. Er zijn wel meerdere kleine stilistische en formele problemen die een hoger cijfer verhinderen. In de discussie staat een duidelijke doublure van een volledige zin, wat slordig oogt. Er zijn ook wat onhandige formuleringen, kleine grammaticale onzuiverheden en APA-inconsistenties in de literatuurlijst en referenties, bijvoorbeeld hoofdlettergebruik, interpunctie, cursivering en enkele onregelmatigheden in bronvermelding. De layout van tabel/figuurpresentatie in de aangeleverde tekst is ook niet volledig netjes. Deze fouten belemmeren het begrip niet, maar maken de stijl minder verzorgd dan bij een echt sterke 8 of hoger. Al met al is dit een degelijke, bovengemiddeld leesbare tekst met enkele merkbare slordigheden.

intro_feedback: De introductie is duidelijk bovengemiddeld voor dit cursusniveau. De maatschappelijke relevantie wordt vroeg en concreet uitgewerkt, de onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen zijn helder geformuleerd, en alle vier vereiste artikelen zijn aanwezig. Sterk is vooral dat theorie (Clark & Wells, inhibitory learning, autonomie/presence) niet alleen genoemd wordt, maar ook gebruikt wordt om de vergelijking tussen zelfgeleide VRET, therapeut-geleide VRET en in vivo exposure te onderbouwen. De eerdere studies worden doorgaans als bouwstenen ingezet en de student positioneert het eigen onderzoek goed ten opzichte van een concrete lacune: de rol van begeleiding binnen VRET. Daardoor voldoet de introductie aan de kerncriteria van Tier 3. Wat nog net ontbreekt voor een excellent niveau is een nog strakkere, volledig naadloze argumentatieve lijn: sommige theoretische onderdelen zijn wat uitgebreid of licht speculatief, en niet alle mogelijke tegenargumenten worden echt vooraf geadresseerd. Maar binnen de context van tweedejaarsstudenten is dit een sterke introductie.
methods_feedback: De methodesectie is voldoende tot adequaat, maar duidelijk minder sterk dan de introductie en discussie. Positief is dat participanten, interventies en procedure allemaal aanwezig zijn, dat de designkeuze coherent is met de onderzoeksvraag, en dat randomisatie wordt genoemd. Ook worden de drie condities begrijpelijk van elkaar onderscheiden en is er aandacht voor standaardisatie. Tegelijk ontbreken meerdere onderdelen die volgens de writing guide verwacht worden. In de participantenbeschrijving worden wel geplande leeftijdsgrenzen en geslacht/steekproefgrootte genoemd, maar geen feitelijke gemiddelde leeftijd met SD en geen feitelijke genderverdeling van de uiteindelijke steekproef. Beloning/compensatie ontbreekt ook. Bij de LSAS-SR is wel een referentie, itemaantal en scorebereik gegeven, maar geen voorbeelditem; bovendien wordt de vragenlijst vooral op basis van Liebowitz genoemd terwijl voor de self-reportversie een psychometrische bron logischer was geweest. Verder staat in de procedure nog nieuwe informatie die eigenlijk eerder onder materialen of design hoort (zoals ethische goedkeuring en designlabel), en de volledige studieverloopbeschrijving blijft wat beknopt. Daarom haalt deze sectie Tier 2 niet volledig en komt zij uit op een 6.5: degelijk genoeg om het onderzoek te volgen, maar nog niet compleet genoeg voor een hogere score.
results_feedback: De resultatensectie is helder en overwegend passend voor dit niveau. De juiste analyse is gekozen en gerapporteerd, de belangrijkste effecten worden met F-waarden, p-waarden en effectgroottes weergegeven, en de uitkomsten worden op operationeel niveau beschreven. Ook zijn er descriptieve statistieken per conditie en meetmoment, en er wordt melding gemaakt van assumptiecontroles en post-hocvergelijkingen. Dat past goed bij een adequate score. Wat de score beperkt, is dat de sectie niet volledig aansluit bij de sample results/rubricverwachtingen: er ontbreekt een aparte demografische tabel per conditie, er wordt geen outliercheck gerapporteerd, en de assumptierapportage is niet helemaal compleet voor het gekozen design. Omdat er maar twee meetmomenten zijn is sfericiteit niet relevant, maar een expliciete verantwoording daarvan of een iets vollediger structuur had het sterker gemaakt. Daarnaast is de tabel- en figuurpresentatie summier uitgewerkt in de tekst. Al met al is dit een nette, begrijpelijke resultatensectie die rond het cursusgemiddelde tot iets daarboven ligt, maar niet helemaal het niveau van een sterke Tier 3-sectie haalt.
discussion_feedback: De discussie is sterk en vormt samen met de introductie het beste deel van het paper. De student herneemt de onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen duidelijk, interpreteert de resultaten op constructniveau, en legt goed uit dat de afname in sociale angst in alle condities past bij exposure- en inhibitory-learningtheorie. Ook wordt het onverwachte deel van de bevindingen — het ontbreken van verschillen tussen de interventies — serieus besproken, met meerdere plausibele verklaringen zoals de hoge mate van structuur in de zelfgeleide conditie en de mogelijkheid dat de gebruikte maat subtiele verschillen niet oppikte. Dat is precies het soort inhoudelijke interpretatie dat in de rubric gewaardeerd wordt. Daarnaast worden beperkingen specifiek en inhoudelijk besproken, inclusief het ontbreken van follow-up, beperkte generaliseerbaarheid en het ontbreken van procesmaten, en de aanbevelingen voor toekomstig onderzoek sluiten daar logisch op aan. Ook de terugkoppeling naar maatschappelijke relevantie is aanwezig. Voor een nog hogere score zou de discussie als geheel nog iets compacter en strakker als één doorlopend argument kunnen worden geschreven; nu zit er wat herhaling in de openingsalinea en blijft de evaluatie van het theoretisch kader meer ondersteunend dan echt verfijnend of bijstellend. Maar voor tweedejaarsniveau is dit duidelijk bovengemiddeld.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is over het algemeen helder, goed leesbaar en duidelijk wetenschappelijk van toon. De opbouw per sectie is logisch, de meeste paragrafen hebben één centrale focus, en de argumentatieve lijn is meestal goed te volgen. Ook de APA-verwijzingen zijn overwegend bruikbaar en er is duidelijk zorg besteed aan academisch formuleren. Wel zijn er meerdere kleine stijl- en APA-onvolkomenheden die een hogere score beperken: er zijn enkele inconsistenties en slordigheden in referenties, interpunctie en opmaak; de discussie bevat bijvoorbeeld een duidelijke herhaling in de eerste alinea; en sommige zinnen zijn wat lang of redundant. Ook de tabellen/figuurvermelding en enkele literatuurlijstitems zijn niet helemaal strak uitgewerkt. Dat zijn geen zware fouten, maar ze maken dat de taal en stijl eerder adequaat dan echt goed/near-faultless zijn. Daarom past een 7.0 goed.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The paper opens with clear societal relevance, defines SAD, explains why treatment access matters, and narrows toward VRET in a logical hourglass structure. The research gap is explicit: no direct comparison of therapist-guided versus self-guided VRET for SAD in young adults with a waitlist control. The research question and hypotheses are clear and relevant. A clear strength is the breadth of literature and the attempt to integrate both Emotional Processing Theory and the Inhibitory Learning Model into the argument. The three core studies are included and used appropriately. The discussion of self-guided VRET and guidance effects also helps justify the design. What keeps this from a higher grade is that the theoretical framework is somewhat more listed than fully integrated into the specific comparison between guided and self-guided VRET. The logic for why therapist guidance should outperform self-guidance is present, but could have been tied more explicitly and consistently to the theories earlier on. There are also a few small inconsistencies in the target group focus, especially shifts between adolescents and young adults, and some references are used a bit broadly. Still, the line of reasoning is coherent, convincing, and clearly above average.
methods_feedback: The methods are coherent and clearly related to the stated research question and hypotheses, so the section is passable and around average. Participants, conditions, and the overall design are understandable. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are quite detailed and mostly well justified with prior work. Random assignment is mentioned, and the three-arm RCT design fits the aims well. The main limitations are incompleteness and uneven detail. Important sample details are missing, especially condition-specific mean age/SD and gender proportions in the Participants section itself, compensation/reward information, and more concrete allocation details. The materials section gives a usable description of the LSAS-SR and VR hardware/content, but the reporting of the LSAS-SR scoring and cutoff values is inaccurate/awkwardly phrased, and instrument description could be cleaner. The intervention descriptions are reasonable, yet some aspects needed for replication remain vague, such as how progression was standardized, what rating scales the clinician used, and how adherence/completion was monitored in the self-guided group. The procedure is quite brief and misses some chronological detail expected by the writing guide, such as more explicit administration order, session context, and debriefing. No dedicated analyses subsection is provided. Overall, the method is coherent and mostly correct, but not complete enough for a good score.
results_feedback: The results section is mostly correct, complete enough, and generally follows the expected sample structure, which is positive for this course level. It includes a demographics table, a descriptive outcome table, the main mixed ANOVA, basic assumption checks, and post-hoc comparisons. The reporting is understandable and clearly linked to the stated design. The significant interaction is interpreted appropriately, and the operational-level reporting is mostly in place. This is around average to slightly above average, but not quite at the level of the sample results. Several issues limit the grade: the section refers to follow-up assessments even though the design only includes pre- and post-treatment; the waitlist post-treatment SD of 56.00 is striking and not commented on; assumption reporting is minimal and incomplete; effect sizes are absent; and the post-hoc reporting could be more systematic. There are also some formatting/statistical style inconsistencies, but these are not heavily penalized here. Overall, the section is solid and coherent, but lacks the completeness and precision needed for a higher score.
discussion_feedback: The discussion is a clear strength of the paper. It begins with a direct answer to the research question, states that the hypotheses were only partially supported, and summarizes the main pattern correctly. The student engages seriously with the unexpected findings, especially the large waitlist improvement and the non-significant difference between self-guided VRET and waitlist. That is an important positive according to the rubric. The discussion also connects findings back to previous literature and offers multiple possible explanations rather than simply ignoring problematic results. Practical implications and limitations are both included, and the future research suggestions are numerous and generally linked to the study's weaknesses. What keeps the score below the stronger end of the range is that some interpretations are too speculative or overextended. For instance, the developmental explanation about young adults being less independent is not strongly grounded in the presented data, and the sudden gains explanation for the waitlist pattern is interesting but somewhat asserted beyond what the design can support. The link back to the theoretical framework is present but relatively brief; the paper mentions expectancy violation and therapist support, but does not deeply evaluate what the findings mean for Emotional Processing Theory versus the Inhibitory Learning Model. Some implications are stronger than the data warrant given the unusual waitlist effect. Still, the section shows good scientific reasoning and is above average for this level.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and scientifically framed, and the overall structure is clear. The reader can follow the argument from introduction through discussion, and paragraphing is mostly functional. This supports a passing grade. However, the language and style are not consistently polished. There are frequent small grammar, punctuation, and formatting problems, including spacing issues, inconsistent capitalization, occasional awkward phrasing, and several APA/reference errors. Some examples include inconsistent study years/names, punctuation around citations, and formatting issues in tables and headings. There is also some redundancy, especially in the discussion and future research sections, where similar points are repeated in slightly different forms. A few sentences are vague or imprecise, but not to the point of obscuring meaning. Overall, the writing is adequate for this course level, but not yet near-faultless.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The research question and hypotheses are clearly stated, the societal relevance is established early, and the paper uses the required articles as part of a visible line of reasoning toward the study aim. A clear strength is that the student does more than summarize individual studies: prior work is generally connected to the broader issue of whether therapist guidance matters in VRET, and the design choice of comparing therapist-guided, self-guided, and waitlist conditions is explicitly justified as filling a gap. Theoretical frameworks are present through Emotional Processing Theory and the Inhibitory Learning Model, and these are linked to the expected benefit of therapist guidance. The introduction also positions the study in a younger population, which helps motivate the design. The main reason this does not move higher is that the argument is not fully tight throughout. Some parts become somewhat list-like, the societal relevance is not always perfectly aligned with the actual studied population because the text shifts between adolescents and young adults, and some transitions could be sharper. There are also a few small inaccuracies/inconsistencies in study details and names. Still, judged against the rubric and expected level, this is clearly above average and fits well in Tier 3.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is broadly coherent and sufficient to understand the intended study, so it passes comfortably. Participants, Materials, and Procedure are all present, the sample size and overall age information are reported, inclusion and exclusion criteria are fairly detailed, and random allocation is described. The independent variable conditions are understandable, and the overall design matches the research question and hypotheses. However, the section remains only adequate because several rubric-required details are missing or incomplete. The Participants section does not report gender distribution there, only later in the Results table, and compensation/reward is not mentioned. The questionnaire description is partly solid but not complete enough for a higher score: the LSAS-SR reference is given and item/scoring details are included, but the cut-off reporting is confusingly phrased and there is no reliability/validity information. Materials and Procedure are also not perfectly separated; treatment-session details sit under Materials, while Procedure is very brief and does not describe the full study from recruitment to debriefing in much detail. There are also no extra materials described for monitoring anxiety despite that being mentioned in the therapist-guided condition. So the section meets Tier 1 clearly and much of Tier 2 in substance, but because some core Tier 2 checklist elements are incomplete, the score stays at the lower end of adequate.
results_feedback: The Results section is solid and clearly modeled on the sample structure, which is appropriate for this assignment. The correct test is used for the stated design, descriptive statistics are reported at the operational level, a demographics table and outcome table are included, assumption checks are mentioned, outliers are addressed, and post-hoc tests with Holm correction are reported. These are all important strengths and support an adequate score. The main limitations are in completeness and precision. The text refers to follow-up assessments when the described design only includes pre- and post-treatment, which creates a notable inconsistency. The assumption checks are reported only briefly and not completely at the level expected for Tier 3. Table/figure formatting is not fully polished, and the waitlist post-treatment SD of 56.00 looks strikingly unusual without comment. Effect sizes are missing, and reporting contains minor APA/statistical inconsistencies. Overall, this is a good student-level Results section that reaches Tier 2, but it does not fully meet the stronger completeness and correctness standard of Tier 3.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion is one of the stronger parts of the paper. The student clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and explains that the hypotheses were only partially supported. The main findings are interpreted at construct level, and the surprising self-guided versus waitlist pattern is not ignored but discussed at length. The discussion also compares findings to prior studies from the introduction and attempts to explain discrepancies, especially the unexpectedly large waitlist improvement. There is a serious effort to connect the findings back to theory by referring to expectancy violation and therapist support. Limitations are specific rather than generic, and future research suggestions mostly follow logically from them. Practical implications are also tied back to the original societal motivation. The main reason the score does not go higher is that the reasoning is not always equally strong across the section. Some interpretations are too speculative or asserted too confidently given the data, especially the developmental explanation and the sudden-gains interpretation for the waitlist group. The theoretical evaluation remains somewhat brief and does not fully work through whether the data support or challenge the two models introduced earlier. The structure is also a bit uneven, with some language and formatting issues interrupting the flow. Still, this is above average and fits Tier 3 overall.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and scientifically phrased, with a clear overall structure and mostly purposeful paragraphs. The writing supports the argument well enough for a passing-to-adequate score. There are also positive features: section headings are helpful, most paragraphs have a recognizable focus, and the tone is mostly appropriate for a psychology paper. However, there are enough language and APA issues to keep this from a higher mark. There are repeated spelling, punctuation, capitalization, spacing, and formatting inconsistencies (for example around citations, commas, p-values, capitalization of terms, and merged headings such as 'LimitationsSeveral'). Some study names and years are inconsistent, and reference formatting contains multiple errors. A few sentences are awkward or imprecise, and some paragraphs are longer and less controlled than ideal. These issues do not usually obscure meaning, so they should not heavily lower content grades, but they do matter here in the Language & Style score. Overall, this is adequately clear and structured, but not polished.

intro_feedback: The Introduction is above average for this course level. It clearly establishes the societal relevance of SAD, explains why treatment access and dropout matter, and develops a coherent argument toward the research question. Theoretical concepts such as cognitive bias, avoidance, inhibitory learning, and reconsolidation are used to justify why VRET may help and why FNE is an important outcome. The three required core studies are discussed, plus an additional study, and these are generally linked to the student’s proposed design rather than being only summarized. The aim, research question, design, and hypotheses are all explicitly stated. The main strengths are the strong relevance argument and the clear narrowing toward FNE as the key construct. The main limitations are that some reasoning becomes overstated or speculative, some claims about prior studies and what exactly they imply are not always fully precise, and the literature synthesis could be tighter in places. The argument is good and convincing overall, but not yet consistently very sharp or parsimonious enough for an excellent score.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and related to the stated research question and hypotheses, so it is clearly a pass. The Participants section gives recruitment route, age range, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and random allocation. The Materials section includes the main outcome measure with developer, number of items, response scale, scoring range, and cut-off, which matches the writing guide reasonably well. The Procedure gives a chronological overview and describes the intervention conditions in substantial detail. However, the section is only around adequate to slightly above average because several required details are missing or underdeveloped. Mean age and SD and gender proportions are not reported in Participants itself, but only later in Results. The Materials section is limited: the VR intervention is not really described there as a material, and the homework worksheets are too vaguely specified to support replication. Reliability/validity information is absent, which is optional but would have strengthened the section. There is also some overlap between Procedure and Materials, and parts of the rationale for inclusion criteria appear in Procedure rather than where they fit best. Most importantly, the waitlist condition and exact implementation details are somewhat less developed than the active conditions. Overall, this is a coherent and mostly correct Methods section, but it lacks some completeness and clean organization expected for a higher grade.
results_feedback: The Results section is solidly adequate and reasonably close to the expected structure from the sample, though not as complete or polished. A demographics table and an outcome table are included, the main analysis matches the design, assumptions are addressed, and the mixed ANOVA and post-hoc results are reported in understandable language. The reporting is coherent enough for this student level, and the interpretation of the interaction is correctly linked to the pattern in the means. This section loses points because it remains somewhat incomplete compared with the sample standard. The assumption checks are mentioned rather briefly and somewhat imprecisely, effect sizes are absent, and the reporting of post-hoc comparisons is not always very neat or fully transparent. The opening sentence about analyzing '180 difference scores' is conceptually awkward given that a mixed ANOVA was performed on repeated measures rather than only on difference scores. Also, the figure is referenced but not actually shown here, and some phrasing/statistical formatting is inconsistent. Still, the core analysis is relevant, mostly correct, and understandable, which keeps this section in the average-to-above-average range.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion is one of the stronger parts of the paper. It opens with a clear answer to the research question, distinguishes between supported and unsupported expectations, and interprets the main findings rather than merely repeating them. The student connects the findings back to prior studies and theory, especially around FNE, context-dependency, and the possible role of real-world exposure. Unexpected findings are not ignored; instead, the discussion tries to explain why VRET alone may have shown effects contrary to expectations. The section also includes meaningful limitations and future research directions that follow from the findings, especially regarding follow-up measurement and variation in VR scenario characteristics. These are study-specific rather than purely generic. The main reason this is not higher is that some interpretations are still too confident relative to the strength of the data, particularly when practical implications are drawn from a null difference between the two active treatments. There is also some imprecision, for example calling the reductions 'clinically significant' when only statistical significance is reported, and the theoretical implications could have been developed more explicitly at the framework level. Overall, though, this is a coherent and above-average Discussion for a second-year paper.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable, uses mostly appropriate scientific language, and has a clear overall structure. Paragraphing is mostly functional, and the line of argument can be followed from Introduction to Discussion. This supports a passing to average Language & Style score. However, there are enough issues to keep the grade from being higher. There are multiple wording and grammar problems, some awkward or overly long sentences, inconsistent terminology, and noticeable APA/reference issues. Examples include the title/header formatting, the section heading 'Discussions' instead of 'Discussion', irregular spacing and punctuation, some citation inconsistencies, and a number of stylistic redundancies. In Results especially, some statistical phrasing is clunky. These issues do not seriously obstruct understanding, so this should not be penalized in content sections, but they do lower the Language & Style score. Overall, the writing is sufficiently clear for this level, but not polished.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The paper clearly states a relevant research question and explicit hypotheses, includes all required articles plus an additional article, and builds a recognizable argument from societal relevance to theory, prior research, gap, and proposed design. A clear strength is that the student does more than summarize studies: Kampmann, Anderson, Bouchard, and Zainal are used as building blocks in an argument about fear of negative evaluation as a specific problem within VRET. Theoretical ideas about cognitive bias, avoidance, inhibitory learning, and context dependence are connected to the hypothesis in a meaningful way. The design is also explicitly justified in relation to prior limitations. What keeps this section below the excellent range is that the reasoning is not always fully tight: some claims are overstated or somewhat speculative, some transitions are still a bit long-winded, and a few conceptual steps are not fully precise. There are also some inaccuracies or loose phrasing around what exactly prior studies showed and how directly theory supports each design choice. Still, this is clearly above average and fits well in the good range.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and clearly related to the research question, and the interventions are described in substantial detail. The differences between VRET standalone and VRET plus homework are generally understandable, and the allocation to conditions and compensation are mentioned. However, several rubric-required elements are missing or not placed well enough to move this section into the adequate range. The Participants subsection does not report mean age with SD or gender distribution there; those details only appear later in Results, so Tier 1 participants criteria are not fully met as written in the Methods. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are present, but justification is mixed into the Procedure. The Materials section only properly describes one questionnaire and does not give comparable detail for all materials; the VR equipment and homework materials are named, but not described at the level expected by the guide. Important information is also misplaced: the Procedure introduces new references and contains a lot of materials-level detail. There is duplication across sections as well. So, despite a solid grasp of the planned study, the section remains around passing rather than adequate.
results_feedback: This Results section is around adequate. The student chooses the correct general analysis for the design, reports the main effects and interaction with statistics and p-values, includes a demographics table, gives means and SDs per condition and time, and reports post-hoc comparisons with Holm correction. There is also an outlier check and mention of assumptions. These are important strengths and align with the sample structure at a basic level. What keeps the grade from the good range is that the reporting is not fully complete or fully careful. Assumption checks are described too globally rather than specifically, and no actual assumption test values are given. The outlier decision is stated, but the rationale is somewhat weakly phrased. Table formatting is rough, and the figure is announced but not actually visible in the submitted text. There are also some inconsistencies in wording, such as discussing 'difference scores' while then running a mixed ANOVA on repeated measurements. In addition, the interpretation in the Results section becomes slightly evaluative at the end, which belongs more in the Discussion. Overall, though, the section is understandable and meets the expected student-level baseline reasonably well.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong discussion for a second-year student. The paper clearly revisits the research question, states that the hypothesis was only partly supported, and interprets the main findings at the construct level rather than only repeating statistics. A major strength is that the student engages seriously with the unexpected result that VRET alone also reduced fear of negative evaluation. The discussion compares findings substantively with prior studies, especially Kampmann, Bouchard, Anderson, and Zainal, and uses theory about context dependency and inhibitory learning to explain discrepancies. The section also includes specific limitations and corresponding future directions, especially regarding VR scenario characteristics and the lack of follow-up. The broader relevance for treatment accessibility is clearly brought back in. What prevents a higher score is that some claims remain somewhat too confident given the study design, and alternative interpretations are not systematically evaluated in depth. Some reasoning is also a bit repetitive. Still, the discussion is clearly above average and fits the good range well.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and appropriately scientific in tone. Most paragraphs have a recognizable focus, the overall structure follows the expected paper format, and references are consistently used. The writing supports the argument reasonably well, especially in the introduction and discussion. However, there are enough language and style issues to keep this in the adequate rather than good range. Sentences are sometimes long and overloaded, which affects precision. There are multiple awkward formulations, occasional grammatical issues, inconsistent terminology, and some typos or formatting problems (for example heading/form layout issues, 'Discussions' instead of 'Discussion,' spacing/punctuation inconsistencies, and a few citation/name inconsistencies such as Moscovitch/Moskovitch). APA is mostly acceptable at student level, but not especially polished. Overall this is solidly understandable and above the passing range, but not yet near-faultless.

intro_feedback:
The introduction is clearly above average for this course level. It starts with societal relevance, explains why SAD is important and why home-based alternatives may matter, and then builds toward a focused comparison between therapist-led and self-led VR. The theoretical framing is relevant and mostly well integrated: cognitive theory, conditioning/extinction, and the role of safety behaviors are all linked to the hypothesis rather than merely listed. The required core studies are discussed and compared in a logical order, and the student generally uses them as building blocks toward the research question. The final aim and hypothesis are clearly stated.

What keeps this from a higher grade is that some parts still read a bit more like strong summary than full synthesis. For example, the argument that therapist guidance specifically improves long-term outcomes is plausible, but the line from theory to this exact design could have been sharpened further. The additional literature on self-led VR is useful, but the introduction could have connected methodological differences across studies even more explicitly to the present design choices. There are also a few inaccuracies/sloppiness issues in references and study descriptions, but they do not fundamentally undermine the reasoning. Overall, this is a coherent and convincing introduction with a clear storyline and relevant hypothesis.
methods_feedback:
The Methods section is coherent and clearly related to the research question and hypotheses. Participants, materials, procedure, and treatment are all present, and the reader can generally understand what was done. Important basics are included: recruitment, inclusion/exclusion criteria, random assignment, sample characteristics, the main outcome measure, diagnostic interview, treatment conditions, number and duration of sessions, and follow-up timing. For this student level, the study is reasonably replicable.

The main reason the grade stays around average rather than clearly above average is that several details are underdeveloped or somewhat inconsistent with the writing guide. The materials section is relatively thin for the intervention itself: the VR software and equipment are named, but the operationalization of the treatment is not described with much precision, especially for the cognitive therapy component. It also remains somewhat unclear how standardized the self-led and therapist-led conditions really are beyond general statements. The LSAS-SR is described reasonably well, but there is a content error in calling it a screening tool for generalized anxiety disorder instead of social anxiety disorder. Allocation is described, but important procedural details such as exact handling of blinding beyond diagnosis, adherence monitoring, and how individualized scenario order was decided could be clearer. Some content that might fit better under Materials is placed under Procedure/Treatment. So overall this is a complete and coherent Methods section, but not yet especially precise or polished.
results_feedback:
The Results section is solid and close to the expected sample structure, which is a strong point. It includes a demographics table, descriptive statistics for the main outcome across conditions and time points, the main mixed ANOVA, assumption checking, reporting of the interaction, and post-hoc comparisons. The reporting is easy to follow and matches the design well. For this course level, that places the section above average.

The section does not go higher because some reporting remains somewhat basic and not fully polished. The student reports assumption checks, but not as comprehensively as in the sample, and some details are selective. Effect sizes are absent, and the reporting occasionally stays at a general level rather than fully operational. The figure is mentioned but not actually shown here, so it cannot strengthen the section. There are also minor statistical/APA issues, such as wording around 'average scores' and some limited precision in the rationale for handling violated assumptions. Still, the core analysis is relevant, coherent, and mostly correct, and the student follows the expected reporting style reasonably well.
discussion_feedback:
The Discussion is one of the stronger parts of the paper. It opens with a clear answer to the research question, states that the hypothesis was partly supported, and distinguishes expected from unexpected findings. The student then relates the findings back to prior literature and theory in a meaningful way rather than merely repeating results. The interpretation of the unexpected maintenance of self-led gains is especially valuable: the student proposes a plausible explanation based on broader exposure scenarios and transfer/generalization, and links this to fear extinction literature.

The critical reflection is also stronger than average. The student does not just list generic limitations, but discusses clinically important issues such as the modest magnitude of improvement, possible regression to the mean, lack of a waiting-list control, and inability to monitor engagement in self-led exposure. These limitations are then connected to specific future research directions. The paper also returns to broader implications and societal relevance at the end, which fits the hourglass model well.

What prevents an even higher grade is that some interpretations go a little beyond the data. For example, suggestions about severe SAD and spontaneous symptom reduction are thoughtful, but somewhat speculative given the design. The theoretical reflection is good, yet it could be a bit more explicit about which parts of the framework were directly tested and which were not. Even so, this is a coherent, well-argued, and above-average discussion for a second-year first paper.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally clear, readable, and appropriately scientific in tone. Paragraphs mostly have a clear focus, and the overall structure is easy to follow. The argument is signposted well enough that the reader can see how the paper moves from problem, to theory and prior research, to method, findings, and implications. This supports a solid language/style grade.

The section is not higher because there are several noticeable APA, formatting, and precision issues. The title page/header information is messy and contains obvious formatting problems. The references contain multiple inconsistencies and errors in APA style, including year mismatches, punctuation issues, irregular journal formatting, duplicated Wang references, and some incorrect citation details. There are also a few awkward phrasings and minor inaccuracies in terminology. These issues do not impede understanding, so they should not drag down content grades, but they do matter here. Overall, the writing is stronger than average in clarity, but the APA/style execution is only moderately polished.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. The research question and hypothesis are clearly stated, societal relevance is introduced early and aligned with the population, and the paper uses the required articles as building blocks rather than only summarizing them one by one. A clear theoretical framework is present: cognitive and behavioral accounts of SAD are linked to why VR exposure should work and why therapist guidance might outperform self-led treatment. The student also positions the study well relative to prior research, especially by using Anderson, Kampmann, Bouchard, and Lindner to motivate the comparison and long-term focus. What keeps this from the excellent range is that the argument is not fully seamless throughout: some parts still read slightly like literature review blocks rather than one completely tight argument, and the design justification could be even more explicitly connected to each identified gap. Still, this is above average and convincingly argued.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is broadly coherent and clearly linked to the research question. Participants are described with sample size, age, gender, inclusion/exclusion criteria, allocation, and reimbursement. The intervention conditions are also described clearly enough to understand what differs between therapist-led and self-led VR, and the session structure is specified. However, the section misses some elements needed for a higher score. Questionnaire/instrument descriptions are incomplete: the SCID-5 is named but not described in the same level of detail as the guide expects, and the VR software/intervention description lacks some standardization details. In addition, important information is placed in a separate 'Treatment' subsection rather than fully integrated under Materials/Procedure as the writing guide suggests, and Procedure introduces some material-related details. The LSAS-SR description is mostly good, though there is a content mistake in calling it a screening tool for generalized anxiety disorder instead of social anxiety disorder. Overall, this is an adequate Methods section, but not yet a strong one.
results_feedback: The Results section is solid and understandable. The correct general analysis is used for the stated design, and the key results are reported at the operational level with test statistics and p-values. The section includes a demographics table, descriptive means and SDs per condition and time point, outlier reporting, and post-hoc tests with Holm correction. This is clearly above passing and roughly around the expected sample-based structure. The main weakness is in the assumptions reporting: not all assumption checks are reported completely or correctly at the level expected for a stronger score. For example, sphericity and normality are stated as met, but there is little detail, and if sphericity was met it is somewhat unclear why corrected degrees of freedom are reported. Figure formatting also cannot be fully evaluated from the text as presented. Effect sizes are absent. So this section is adequate and close to the course sample, but not strong enough for the good tier.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong Discussion. The student clearly returns to the research question, states whether the hypothesis was supported, and interprets the findings at the construct level. The discussion compares the results to prior studies in a substantive way rather than only listing them, and it does a good job explaining the unexpected maintenance of gains in the self-led condition by linking this to methodological differences and extinction/generalization theory. The theoretical framework from the introduction is meaningfully revisited, especially around fear extinction, cognitive change, and the role of therapist support. Limitations are specific and relevant: lack of a waiting-list control and inability to assess engagement in the self-led condition are both discussed in relation to how they affect interpretation. Future research suggestions are specific and logically derived. What prevents a higher mark is that some claims become a bit speculative, especially around spontaneous recovery/regression to the mean and the inference about severe SAD, and the broader theoretical contribution is solid rather than especially original. Still, this is a good, above-average discussion.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is clearly readable and generally well structured. Paragraphs mostly have a single focus, transitions are usually smooth, and scientific language is used appropriately. The writing supports the argument well enough for this level. There are, however, several APA and presentation issues that keep this from the good tier: formatting is inconsistent in places, there are errors in the title page/header information, some references contain inaccuracies or inconsistent formatting, and a few wording issues reduce precision. There are also some small awkward phrasings and citation inconsistencies. Because the text remains clear and coherent throughout, these problems do not severely hurt the score, but they do keep it in the adequate range.

intro_feedback:
The introduction is clearly present and has a recognizable storyline from societal relevance to theory, prior research, and the study aim. A strong point is that the student does more than list studies: they try to build an argument from exposure theory to VR exposure and then to the potential added value of group delivery. The research question and hypothesis are stated clearly at the end, and the relevance of comparing group VR, individual VR, and waitlist is understandable. The student also includes the required core studies and generally uses references responsibly.

The main reason this is not higher is that the argumentation is only somewhat convincing rather than fully strong. Some literature use is inaccurate or awkwardly framed. For example, Anderson et al. (2013) is characterized in a way that overstates what it can show for the present comparison, and the sequence of Bouchard, Ørskov, Kampmann, and Anderson does not always function as tight building blocks. The theoretical framework is present, especially around maladaptive cognitions, avoidance, and inhibitory learning, but it remains somewhat simplified and not always sharply linked to the exact design choices. There are also several questionable source choices for key claims, such as web pages or broad clinical sources where stronger empirical sources would have been preferable. Still, for a second-year first paper, the line of reasoning is coherent and the study is well motivated overall, which places this around adequate to good.
methods_feedback:
The methods section is complete enough to understand the intended study and broadly replicate it at student level. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present. The design matches the research question: three conditions, pre-post measurement, and randomized allocation. The treatment conditions are described in a reasonably understandable way, and the LSAS-SR is named, referenced, briefly explained, and scored. The procedure is chronological and generally clear.

The main limitation is that several important details are vague, inconsistent, or placed a bit imprecisely. The participant description is incomplete: the mean age appears to be missing its value, only SD is shown, and the inclusion/exclusion criteria are confusingly phrased ('no older than three years old', 'current use of pharmacological therapy, not older than a year'). It is not fully clear how diagnosis was established in practice, who assessed it, or how exclusion criteria were checked. In Materials, the description mixes treatment content and procedure, and the active conditions are said to include cognitive restructuring despite the introduction emphasizing exposure more specifically. The psychometric information for the LSAS-SR is minimal, and reliability/validity are only vaguely mentioned. Analytic choices are not really described in the Methods, which is a missed opportunity even if the Results section later reports them. So the section is coherent and mostly correct, but not detailed or polished enough for a clearly 'good' score.
results_feedback:
The results section follows the sample structure fairly closely, which is a clear strength. It begins with sample use and outliers, presents descriptive statistics, reports assumption checks, gives the mixed ANOVA results, and follows up with Holm-corrected post hoc comparisons. The findings are understandable and relevant to the stated design. The core interpretation is clear: both active conditions improved, the waitlist did not, and group VR did not significantly differ from individual VR.

This section is around the expected benchmark for a solid student-level Results section, but not higher. The reporting is mostly correct and complete, yet there are some issues. The descriptive tables are not optimally formatted and Table 1 combines outcome descriptives with assumption checks in a cluttered way. The demographic reporting is incomplete relative to the sample template: gender frequencies are given, but age descriptives by condition are missing, and the note that age is omitted is not ideal. There is also some inconsistency in table numbering and presentation, and the figure is mentioned but not actually shown in the submitted text. In addition, an age covariate appears in later ANOVA tables without being introduced in the analysis plan, which creates some conceptual confusion. These issues keep it below a stronger 'good' score, but overall the analyses and reporting are coherent and appropriate for this level.
discussion_feedback:
The discussion is one of the stronger sections. It opens with a clear restatement of the aim, research question, and hypotheses, then directly answers them. The student distinguishes between the supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis and gives a plausible interpretation of why group VR did not outperform individual VR. The discussion also connects the findings back to inhibitory learning and expectancy violation theory, and it uses prior research to situate both the expected and unexpected results. The broader implication that VR exposure seems useful in both formats is reasonably argued from the data.

The section also includes multiple limitations and links them to future research, which is good. The limitation about insufficient interpersonal processes in the group condition is study-specific and relevant, and the absence of follow-up is also well noted. However, the critical reflection is not always equally convincing. Some claims become speculative, especially when explaining age-related differences in technological fluency, because these were not directly tested and age did not appear to matter in the reported analysis. The discussion of theoretical implications is present but not very deep: it suggests that VR itself may be sufficiently potent, but it does not fully refine the theory or clearly separate which mechanisms were tested versus assumed. Practical implications are somewhat broad and positive, with only limited caution about the modest scope of the design. Still, the reasoning is coherent, relevant, and above average for this level.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and the overall structure is clear. Sections are in the expected order, most paragraphs have a recognizable focus, and the reader can usually follow the argument. The scientific tone is mostly appropriate for this level, and the student uses relevant terminology consistently enough.

However, there are enough language, style, and APA issues to keep this below average-to-adequate rather than strong. There are many sentence-level awkward phrasings, punctuation problems, spacing issues, and grammatical slips. Some examples include inconsistent capitalization, unnecessary repetition, and unclear formulations. APA/reference quality is mixed: there are formatting problems, some incorrect source details, odd citation choices for central claims, and a few likely errors in titles or journals. The front matter also contains obvious placeholder or nonsensical information (date and word count), which hurts professionalism and layout. These issues do not make the paper incomprehensible, so this is not insufficient, but they are too frequent for a higher language/style score.

intro_feedback: This is a strong introduction for this course level. It clearly states the research question and hypothesis, addresses societal relevance early, includes the required studies, and builds a recognizable line of reasoning toward the design. A particular strength is that the student does more than summarize articles: the studies are used as steps in an argument about why comparing group VR with individual VR is a logical next step. The theoretical framework is also present and linked to the hypothesis through concepts such as maladaptive cognitions, avoidance, expectancy violation, and inhibitory learning. The design choice is explicitly justified with reference to gaps in prior work. What keeps this from the excellent range is that the argument is not fully tight throughout: some transitions are a bit forced, some claims are overstated or only loosely supported, and there are some content inaccuracies and imprecise use of sources. In addition, the societal relevance is somewhat broad rather than sharply tailored to the exact design and population. Still, this is clearly above average and fits well in Tier 3.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is broadly coherent and passes comfortably, but it has several omissions that keep it around the adequate range. Strengths are that the sample size, age information, gender distribution, inclusion/exclusion criteria, reward, allocation method, conditions, and general procedure are all described. The design is also coherent with the research question. The independent variable conditions are understandable, and the waitlist is clearly explained. However, the questionnaire description is incomplete relative to the writing guide: the reference is given and the number of items, scale, example item, and score range are reported, but interpretation is limited and psychometric information is very brief. More importantly, not all required details are consistently presented with enough precision. Some participant criteria are awkward or unclear ('DSM-5 diagnosis no older than three years old', medication 'not older than a year'), and materials and procedure are somewhat mixed together. The intervention description is sufficient to understand the study, but not detailed enough for a stronger replication standard even at this student level. Overall, this is adequate but not yet a strong Methods section.
results_feedback: The Results section is solid and broadly follows the expected sample-based structure. The student reports the correct analysis for the design, includes descriptive statistics, reports main effects and the interaction with test statistics and p-values, includes assumption checks, mentions outliers with a decision to retain them, and reports Holm-corrected post-hoc comparisons. This matches many Tier 2 expectations. A further strength is that effect sizes are included in some tables. The main reason this does not reach the good range is that some expected elements are incomplete or not cleanly presented. The demographics table is incomplete for rubric purposes because age per condition is not clearly reported in a demographic table. Some formatting is messy, table labelling is inconsistent, and Figure 1 is referenced but not actually shown in the submitted text. In addition, the normality discussion is incomplete because one Shapiro-Wilk test at post for the waitlist appears significant, yet this is not really handled. So the section is understandable and above passing, but not fully complete or polished enough for Tier 3.
discussion_feedback: This is a strong Discussion and one of the better parts of the paper. The student clearly revisits the aim and hypothesis, answers the research question, and interprets the findings at the construct level rather than merely repeating statistics. The discussion meaningfully connects findings to prior literature, especially Kampmann et al. and Anderson et al., and uses the theoretical framework to explain why both active VR formats may have worked. A notable strength is that the unexpected finding that group VR did not outperform individual VR is directly addressed rather than ignored. The limitations are also relatively specific and linked to the conclusions, and the future directions follow logically from those limitations. The section also returns to broader practical relevance at the end. What prevents a higher mark is that some interpretations are still somewhat speculative and not always weighed against alternatives in a fully critical way. There is also some repetition, and the broader research context beyond the studies already discussed remains limited. Nevertheless, the reasoning is coherent and convincingly argued for this level, so this fits Tier 3 well.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally understandable and structured, and most paragraphs have a recognizable focus. The overall scientific register is present, and the reader can follow the main argument. However, language and APA quality are below the level of the stronger content sections. There are frequent grammar and phrasing problems, awkward sentence constructions, punctuation issues, capitalization inconsistencies, and multiple reference inaccuracies. Some examples include imprecise wording, citation and formatting errors, inconsistent article titles or source types, and table formatting problems. There are also some odd presentation issues in the title page information and metadata. These issues do not usually obscure meaning, so the paper remains readable, but they are too frequent for the adequate-to-good range.
